item.title: Maybe Goldman Sachs' Asian equities traders won't be so quick to join hedge funds now?
item.description:
Goldman Sachs' Asian equities business is having a great year. Equities revenues at the firm globally were up 50% year-on-year in the half of 2026, with the Asian equities business the standout performer. Speaking to CNBC <https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/01/goldman-traders-are-on-pace-for-a-record-year-a-close-up-look-at-how-theyre-doing-it.html>in early August, Kevin Kelly, the firm's global co-head of equities said the Asian franchise has been benefitting from a "multiyear investment" in both traders and technology.
This may be so, but Goldman's Asian equity business has also suffered some exits, particularly to major hedge funds. Now something has occurred that may make its investments think twice about leaving.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-04/citadel-s-asia-head-of-trading-is-leaving-after-just-four-months?srnd=all> reported earlier today that AJ Bolduc, who left Goldman Sachs to join Citadel as head of Asia trading and primary strategies in February, has left again. After gardening leave, Bolduc only joined in May and so was there only four months. It is not clear why she left so soon. Bolduc did not respond to a request to comment. Citadel declined to comment.
Goldman Sachs appears to have liked Bolduc. It hired her from Macquarie in 2018 and promoted her to managing director </news/goldman-sachs-managing-directors-2025> in January 2026. She left for Citadel two months later.
Bolduc may have moved on from Citadel of her own accord. Either way, Ed Philips, whom Citadel hired from UBS in March 2025 and who is currently based in London, will now be managing Citadel's Asia trading and primary strategies instead.
Bolduc's departure is likely to give other members of Goldman's Asian equities team pause for thought. Insiders say there have been multiple departures to funds, including those of Abby Dong, a vice president who went to Millennium in June and Minsu Kim, who went to Millennium in March.
Citadel is still hiring in Asia as it builds out its fundamental equities business, but Bolduc's swift arrival and departure is a reminder that hedge fund jobs don't always last. </news/hedge-fund-jobs-are-a-nightmare>

item.title: "I am a first year student who wants to work in banking. I already work 100 hours a week"
item.description:
I am in my first year of studies at a university in London. I want to work in an investment bank </news/what-is-an-investment-bank> when I graduate. I'd love to work in M&A </news/get-a-job-in-ma> or capital markets. </news/capital-markets-jobs-ecm-and-dcm>
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
I appreciate that this is not easy and I am already working very hard on my CV </news/the-absolutely-perfect-investment-banking-cv>. Alongside my studies and a 40 hour job in retail, I run a small start-up with friends at university. On a typical week I am working 100 hours, often more.
The job market is very bad at the moment. I don't come from a family with money and if I can get into banking it will change everything. I can code and I am using agentic AI </news/agentic-ai-for-banking-jobs>to help make my applications. I have already completed a few small internships.
I want this badly. I am confident that I will get a job, but I am also aware that it is a long road and I am already working long hours. I hear nothing back from a lot of the applications I make, even though I have a great cover letter story with a strong narrative about why I am good for banking.
If you have any suggestions or are also going through this process, let me know below.
Nisan Minhas is a pseudonym

item.title: Citi hired a co-head of UK & EMEA DCM from JPMorgan last year. Now he's gone
item.description:
Thirteen months ago, we reported that Citi had hired Rob Cascarino </news/now-citi-hired-jp-morgan-s-former-global-co-head-of-sponsors-private-side-sales> from JPMorgan and made him co-head of debt capital markets for UK and EMEA. Now, it seems that Cascarino has left again.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
The FCA Register says that Cascarino arrived at Citi in London on October 31st 2025. However, the FCA Register also says that Cascarino left Citi's London entities on July 30th 2026.
Where is Cascarino now? Citi declined to comment. Cascarino didn't respond to a request to comment. It's understood that he in fact resigned last week for a new role as a partner at PJT.
Cascarino arrived at Citi after a period of change in the debt capital markets business. He displaced Paul Gibbs, who then left Citi in March 2026. </news/citi-s-london-dcm-team-has-lost-various-people-for-various-reasons>It's also thought that the team was restructured to give origination banks greater dominance over syndicate bankers.
Despite the changes </news/citi-dcm-bankers-fired> and various senior departures </news/citi-s-london-dcm-team-has-lost-various-people-for-various-reasons> in the past 18 months, Citi's EMEA debt capital markets (DCM) business has done well. It ranked third by revenues with a 6% market share behind BNP Paribas and JPMorgan in the first half according to Dealogic. This is thought to be testimony to the strength of the remaining team and to strong VPs and directors.
Only in financial institutions group (FIG) DCM did Citi rank outside the top 10. FIG DCM bankers like Tommaso Ponsele </news/citi-needs-new-dcm-bankers-after-goldman-sachs-curious-hire> and Colm Rainy were among those leaving Citi's team. The bank also lost Piers Davison, the co-head of the European FIG group in late 2022. He's now at Alvarez and Marsall.
It's not clear whether anyone will replace Cascarino. Citi still has Uday Malhotra, Cascarino's co-head of EMEA DCM, who joined from BofA in 2022.

item.title: Morning Coffee: 48-year-old Citadel London trader who generated $2bn profit decides to take things easy. Money honey mystery
item.description:
What does Chris Foster at Citadel do to relax? We cannot say for sure, but he can be seen here <https://www.mansfield.ox.ac.uk/for-mansfield-forever/meet-our-lead-benefactor/>wearing lurid socks and reclining on a chair, so maybe there's a lot of that.
There could be more of this to come. The Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/b4c17a07-f684-44c7-b334-8b7bcb1a21d6?syn-25a6b1a6=1> is reporting that Foster, Citadel's star trader in London, is stepping down. His boss, Sebastian Barrack, who likes climbing mountains for fun, </news/citadel-energy-trading> says he is "grateful" for Foster's leadership and for his "contributions" over a nearly 20 year period.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
The contributions Barrack highlights are building Citadel's European natural gas trading team. The contributions Barrack doesn't highlight are Foster's enormous contributions to profitability, particularly in 2022 when he and his London reportedly <https://www.ft.com/content/3d0842dd-a8f4-435d-b888-5587b4b9eeda?syn-25a6b1a6=1> generated $2bn in profits following the outbreak of war in Ukraine.
Foster was 44-years-old when he made the $2bn. He is 48-years-old now. He joined Citadel from Merrill Lynch in 2008 and he made partner at Citadel in London in 2011, aged 33. The last time we looked, partners at Citadel in London </news/pay-at-hedge-fund-citadel-in-london-500k-to-21mm> were earning $21m each. After the 2022 $2bn, Citadel's partners were paid an average of $70m each. Foster could afford a lot of socks.
In fact, Foster gave £25m of his 2022 windfall to Mansfield College <https://issuu.com/mansfieldoxford/docs/mansfield_magazine_final_issuu_/6?e=9&o=1>, the Oxford College which took him in to study maths after the more prestigious St. John's rejected him. Foster, who came from a state school in Wigan got a first class maths degree from Oxford and supports widening access to elite education. "If I could get a first class maths degree from Oxford, I could do anything," he told the college magazine after making his donation.
Foster won't be retiring from Citadel entirely. He will still be an advisor to Barrack. Trading natural gas isn't easy as it used to be in these volatile times, but Foster seems to have planned his sock-wearing well. Last year, he appointed 42-year-old Stephen Carter and 39-year-old Adam Frame on his team as replacements, both of whom he reportedly hired.
Foster is not the only Citadel natural gas trader to move on. Last year, Eike Schick </news/a-37-year-old-partner-at-hedge-fund-citadel-retired-to-become-a-student> left aged 37 to study a new degree in psychology.
Separately, where is Maria Bartiromo?
Bartiromo, also known as the "Money Honey" has not been seen since August 9th, notes the Wall Street Journal. <https://www.wsj.com/business/media/maria-bartiromo-out-at-fox-news-83dbb6ac?mod=hp_lead_pos9>She has left Fox News, which is saying things <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-03/maria-bartiromo-to-leave-fox-news-after-12-years-at-network?taid=6a99d42007aa2e000164360a&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter> like, "We wish her all the best on her next chapter."
The implication is that Bartiromo, now aged 58, has something else going on. Bloomberg notes that she is a celebrity of financial journalism who has also appeared in films and inspired a punk song.
Meanwhile...
Rogo Technologies, which automates the work of junior bankers, is setting up in Singapore and wants to hire 150 to 200 people there by the end of next year. Nomura, Daiwa and Barclays are using it already. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-26/ai-startup-that-upends-junior-bankers-work-sets-up-in-singapore>
Citadel is up 12.1% year-to-date. Millennium is up 8.2%. Balyasny is only up 0.5%. (Business Insider) <https://www.businessinsider.com/august-hedge-fund-performance-multistrats-millennium-balyasny-2026-9>
What is noticeable about Balyasny’s year is that it appears to be struggling across the board – equities, fixed income and commodities. (Rupak Ghose) <https://rupakghose.substack.com/p/peak-pod-shop-and-balyasny-blues>
Leon Black, formerly of Apollo, says the House Oversight Committee overstepped its authority in summoning him for a deposition on his links to Jeffrey Epstein and is suing the committee. “This is no longer about finding the truth about Epstein. It is about trying to destroy Mr. Black,” says his lawyer. Black denies any wrongdoing. (WSJ) <https://www.wsj.com/politics/policy/leon-black-sues-house-committee-over-epstein-probe-a17aa95c?mod=panda_wsj_author_alert>
“It defies belief that Epstein’s tax advice was worth the vast sums of money Black paid him. No one, and I mean no one, believes that Black’s usual world-class professional advisors needed Epstein’s help to execute routine tax planning structures,” Sen. Wyden said in an emailed statement. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2026-09-03/epstein-tax-advice-payments-focus-of-apollo-s-leon-black-s-house-deposition?taid=6a995c983375640001f248a5&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
Maybe hedge funds won't need weather specialists after all. Google DeepMind has got a new product that forecasts how hard the wind blows at turbine height and how much sunlight reaches a solar farm. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-03/deepmind-s-new-ai-weather-model-goes-hourly-for-power-markets?taid=6a99c03607aa2e00016434c0&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
How to dress during your high profile hedge fund divorce. Laura Overdeck was wearing a gray-and-white striped jacket, white slacks and chunky blue heels. John Overdeck was clad in a navy-blue suit, light blue shirt and no tie. John was sipping organic green tea. (WSJ) <https://www.wsj.com/finance/investing/inside-the-n-j-courtroom-where-a-hedge-fund-titans-messy-divorce-is-playing-out-b9e3ce32>
John Overdeck said that while their three children were growing up, Laura had the help of a full-time nanny who doubled as a personal secretary, and a housekeeper who worked 15 hours a week. He also rarely worked weekends so that he could coach sports teams. (WSJ) <https://www.wsj.com/personal-finance/a-hedge-fund-titans-divorce-is-putting-wall-streets-staggering-wealth-on-public-view-6c419f4c>
The three French founders of Hugging Face, Clement "Clem" Delangue, Julien Chaumond, and Thomas Wolf are now worth after Nvidia agreed to buy Hugging Face. Initially it was supposed to be a chatbot for teenagers. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-03/nvidia-agrees-to-13-billion-deal-for-ai-platform-hugging-face>
Goldman Sachs hired ex-Nomura CTO Dinesh Keswani as CTO for its middle and back office functions. (The Stack) <https://www.thestack.technology/goldman-sachs-poaches-nomuras-global-cto-to-lead-core-engineering/>
State Street has got a new infrared sauna at its London office. (Financial News) <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/an-infrared-sauna-and-an-on-site-gym-fn-visits-state-streets-new-london-hq-f8cb9689s>

item.title: "The problem with hedge funds is that most portfolio managers are no good"
item.description:
I spent much of the past decade of my life working for a hedge fund that ultimately returned money to investors. Based upon my own experience and my observations of other hedge funds in the same situation, there are two common points of failure.
i. Portfolio managers exaggerate their own abilities.
ii. Hedge funds pay them too much.
It has been standard in this industry for portfolio managers joining new funds to demand large guaranteed payments. </news/multistrategy-hedge-funds-pay-millions>This is partly to compensate them for deferred compensation at previous employers, and partly because they will all assure you that they are capable of generating large amounts of PnL.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
This is almost always untrue. A tiny minority of people can consistently make money. And yet portfolio managers are so convinced of their own worth that they will only move if they are paid upfront. You pay them. They don't make the money they said they would, and then you are stuck with a huge cost - and possibly also their loss.
This is why starting a large new hedge fund from scratch is almost impossible now. The cost of finding, hiring, and then integrating high maintenance portfolio managers has become prohibitive. The industry is only viable for established funds that have hired portfolio managers slowly over a period of years. The established funds can afford to add new staff slowly. They can also afford to pay.
This is why life has been tough for many new funds. It's also why taking money from big funds like Millennium </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-hedge-fund-millennium> is becoming the only option. Taking a risk on a lot of new portfolio management talent is not for the faint hearted. Taking a risk on that portfolio management talent while trying to keep a plethora of outside investors happy is an impossibility.
Casper LeGros is a pseudonym

item.title: Deutsche Bank has a new MD in New York. He’s in a hot area
item.description:
Much has been said about how AI is decimating hiring opportunities </news/junior-bankers-ai-jobs>; not as much has been said about the hiring opportunities created by the technology. Luckily, there is at least one role in high demand.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Ren Chen will join Deutsche Bank later this month in New York as a managing director (MD) and global head of its enterprise and AI banking teams. He will initially report to Jeff Cady, Deutsche’s head of Americas banking, and then Ed Lui </news/bank-of-america-m-a>, who is joining Deutsche as global head of technology, media, and telecommunications banking when he joins in November. Deutsche Bank declined a request for comment on this article, and Chen did not respond to a request for comment.
Chen joined Deutsche from Chinese autonomous driving technology company WeRide, where he was chief strategy officer. He was CFO and chief business officer at startup Reka AI before that, for 10 months. Before his time in the industry, Chen spent 14 years at Morgan Stanley </news/2023/11/ren-chen-morgan-stanley>, where he was an MD in its capital markets team and global head of its internet investment banking offering. He worked across New York and Hong Kong for the bank.
“The last 3 years have made me truly believe the transformative change that AI will bring to bear on all aspects of our lives,” Chen said in a social media post. “It's because of this belief that I am headed to Deutsche Bank.”
Technology bankers are in high demand </news/technology-bankers>, and AI bankers are a key part of that. It’s no surprise; JPMorgan estimated last month <https://www.jpmorgan.com/insights/banking/capital-markets/financing-ai-infrastructure-data-centers?utm_source=chatgpt.com> that capital expenditure at the five largest cloud and technology companies will reach $697bn in 2026. That colossal pile of money is a business opportunity for banks, and hires like Chen (and Liu, as we noted) are important for Deutsche Bank, which has just a third of the number </news/highest-paid-bankers> of managing directors that a more-entrenched bank like Goldman Sachs or JPMorgan has.

item.title: One of Jane Street's most important teams is full of professional speed daters
item.description:
Now that AI </news/how-ai-is-affecting-careers-in-electronic-trading-and-hft>makes it easier than ever to structure messy data, sourcing useful alternative data </news/how-ai-is-affecting-careers-in-electronic-trading-and-hft#:~:text=People%20who%20source,of%20the%20chimney.%22> is one of the most important roles in an electronic trading firm. </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm>Eric Mannes, who runs the alternative data team at Jane Street </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-jane-street>, recently appeared on the firm's podcast, Signals and Threads <https://signalsandthreads.com/wrestling-the-world-into-rows/>, to discuss the small, niche team which puts that data in the hands of traders.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Jane Street's alt data team is split into two broad categories: data engineering and data sourcing. Jobs in the latter camp are far more social: sourcers will go around speaking to the desks to understand what kind of data they need, then will attend various events and conferences where vendors pitch their datasets to them. For example, Mannes said that companies like Neudata, which catalogue the various available data sources, run "speed dating" events. Jane Street's data sourcers have "10, 15-minute dates in a row" where vendors explain their datasets, and the sourcers have to decide whether it's useful to any trading desks or whether it's unnecessary noise.
Alt data is a massive field brimming with noise. The most famous example of alt data is satellite imagery, but there are inherent issues and risks to using that kind of data. Mannes said that footage of Walmart parking lots, for example, is "really indirect. The thing you’re getting at is how many people showed up, which is different from how much they’re spending." Documents that a company files with the SEC are more structured and usable, but everyone has them, so you won't get much alpha on that front. The best data sourcers, therefore, should be able to find data that's usable, but obscure enough to give their traders an edge.
The field of usable data is expanding, particularly regarding text data, because of the improvement in large language models which can give structure to unstructured data. There are risks to using LLMs too; because of the massive amount of data they're trained on, there may be subtle biases, especially when backtesting. "The LLM knows what happened to Enron," Mannes said, and might incorporate retrospective knowledge instead of using the information that traders would have actually had at that time.
CTO Ron Minsky confirmed that Jane Street has been building "super smart LLMs that are useful productivity tools," but has ways around that issue. It has a data "Superstore" which, among other things records all the information that Jane Street receives and the context in which it was received so that any retrospective changes to that data are not carried forward.
Jane Street's alt data </news/hedge-funds-and-market-makers-need-data-strategists-as-war-heats-up>team also includes a 20-person contingent of data engineers, who build the pipelines that process its data. Mannes said the team is looking for curious, investigative people; engineering skills are required but the "systems complexity" is not as high as it is in the firm's broader engineering organization. Mannes said people with "science or social science backgrounds, who do work with messy real-world data and try to make sense of it, are well suited to this." The team is also launching an internship track in 2027. </news/this-is-what-it-takes-to-get-a-64k-jane-street-internship>

item.title: Susquehanna's head of prediction markets hired his old friend: an ex-Morgan Stanley trading head
item.description:
In 2006, <https://archive-publications.library.columbia.edu/?a=d&d=cs20061103-01.2.13&e=-------en-20--1--txt-txIN-------->Columbia University student Jeremy Maletz won the third place prize in a poker tournament </news/quant-poker-the-new-path-to-a-job-at-an-electronic-trading-firm> hosted by Susquehanna </news/a-high-frequency-trading-firm-just-hired-bjarne-stroustrup-creator-of-c>, an electronic trading firm. </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm> He joined the firm as a graduate </news/electronic-trading-summer-internship-pay> and worked his way up to become the head of its burgeoning prediction markets </news/prediction-markets-jobs-kalshi-polymarket>team. The Columbia Spectator reported that he was invited alongside his friend Nick Volbi, who subsequently opted for a more traditional career path in banking. Now, however, the pair are reunited.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Nick Volbi joined Susquehanna as its head of institutional prediction markets; his LinkedIn profile says the role involves providing businesses with "bespoke risk transfer" using event contracts on platforms like Kalshi </news/traders-earning-1m-on-kalshi-are-offered-double-or-nothing-to-join-trading-firms> and Polymarket. FINRA's BrokerCheck tool suggests that he joined the firm last Wednesday. Volbi spent most of his career at Morgan Stanley, where he made MD in 2020 and was latterly its head of equity index derivatives trading. He left the bank for BNP Paribas in 2025, where he worked as deputy head of index flow derivatives trading prior to joining Susquehanna.
The Columbia Spectator said Alex Verbuch also attended the tournament with Maletz and Volbi. He too works at Susquehanna as head of trading for the firm's Bahamas-based crypto trading entity. It's not clear whether Maletz and Volbi have remained in touch since the tournament, nor whether Maletz was directly involved in the hiring process. Neither responded to a request for comment.
Speaking on Bloomberg's Odd Lots podcast in June, <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IblwpXSh6xM>Maletz said Susquehanna was one of the earliest firms to enter the prediction markets space and wants to be a "shepherd for other institutions as they get involved." He said that the goal is for institutions to use event contracts to hedge against the real world impacts of the event itself. Susquehanna's founder Jeff Yass said there's also an altruistic element to growing prediction markets. He said on the Generating Alpha podcast last October <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qU9N75Fe1yU> that one use case for prediction markets is to fact check governments; for example, he argued it could prevent wars by giving the public a more accurate prediction for the expected cost of entering into a conflict.
Susquehanna is growing its prediction markets team. It has openings for a trader, software developer and data engineer working on prediction markets in its Philadelphia HQ. It's also hiring a quantitative sports trader in Dublin "focused primarily on trading on prediction markets."

item.title: Colleagues of murdered BofA VP Erin Piacenti help raise nearly $450k for her young child
item.description:
It's three days since Erin Piacenti, </news/erin-piacenti-bank-of-america>a 32-year-old vice president in Bank of America's business selection and conflicts team was stabbed to death near Times Square. Colleagues at the bank have been promoting a GoFundMe <https://www.gofundme.com/f/in-memory-of-erin-piacenti-supporting-madisons-future>for her family, which has already raised nearly $450k.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
The New York Times <https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/01/nyregion/victims-stabbing-times-square-nyc.html> reports that Piacenti had only just returned from five months' maternity leave after having a baby daughter. She was on her way back from Bank of America's nearby office when she was stabbed in the stomach by Pamela Cisneros, a woman with a history of mental health problems. Cisneros, who was subsequently shot and killed by police, reportedly stabbed Piacenti shortly after the BofA VP passed a vendor selling baseball hats and sunglasses. Piacenti tragically died in hospital.
Piacenti's GoFundMe page, states that she returned from maternity leave on August 31st. Over 4,000 people have already donated to her fund, which has a target amount of $750k to help support her daughter, Madison.
Writing on LinkedIn, Yaelle Birman, the global head of business selection and conflicts at Bank of America, said Piacenti's death in a "senseless unprovoked violent attack" had been devastating. "Our BSC team will miss you dearly Erin," said Birman. "We will remember, amongst other things, your bubbly, warm and kind personality as well as your brilliant mind. It was such a gift having you in the team."

item.title: Balyasny's new AI fellowship program could get you a job on a trading desk
item.description:
Hedge funds </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> and trading firms </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm> are building out their 'AI labs </news/optiver-ai-lab>' and applied AI teams. Balyasny has one of the more robust AI teams, but has launched a new program for junior-to-mid level AI professionals </news/the-difference-between-working-as-a-quant-in-finance-and-as-a-researcher-in-an-ai-lab>which could land them a seat on a top trading desk.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Balyasny has created an 'AI Fellowship Program,' based in New York. It's recruiting multiple candidates on a full-time basis to participate in three-month rotations across individual trading teams at the hedge fund; the AI fellow will become "the dedicated AI partner to a portfolio manager," and build new tools for them and their team to use. Before embarking on these rotations, the AI fellows spend a few months with Balyasny's central AI team, which had 20 researchers as of March and is led by Google alum Charlie Flanagan. The role is targeted at masters graduates or above with 3-5 years of experience, and pays a salary of up to $225k.
In principle, the fellowship seems similar to the 'AI accelerators' </news/jp-morgan-paying-325k-salaries-for-its-new-ai-strike-team> seen in banks. JPMorgan established a team earlier this year that would be deployed into different divisions to see how they could benefit from AI. The difference between that and Balyasny's AI fellowship is that the trading desks that the fellows rotate into have "signalled demand for these seats, and the goal is a permanent home on the desk."
Balyasny isn't the only firm hiring applied AI professionals. At Hudson River Trading, where traders have been known to spend $1k per day on AI tokens </news/ai-token-use-traders>, there are four openings for HAIL, its AI lab. Each role is based in either London or New York and offers salaries of up to $300k. In Miami, </news/hedge-funds-are-following-citadel-to-miami-they-re-disappointed-in-the-tech-talent> Citadel Securities is hiring graduates for its centralized applied AI team; the market maker has taken a page out of the books of the major AI labs and has begun referring to people in that team as 'members of technical staff.' </news/top-paying-ai-jobs>

item.title: A JPMorgan infrastructure banker resigned. He is not going to Citi (for now)
item.description:
Two months ago, we suggested </news/jp-morgan-promoted-some-people-who-might-have-moved-to-citi>that Dan Darley, an infrastructure banking managing director (MD) at JPMorgan in London might be on the list of people Citi would like to hire. Now Darley has resigned. But he is not going to Citi after all.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Darley didn't comment for this article, but we understand that he is taking some time out to be with his family and has nothing lined up. That time may last for 12 months or so.
Darley spent 15 years at JPMorgan before leaving on Tuesday this week.
Citi likes to hire JPMorgan bankers. It hired Vlad Ivanov from JPMorgan as co-head of infrastructure banking in EMEA in May. Ivanov spent nearly 24 years at JPMorgan and presumably knows Darley well.
It does not seem inconceivable that Darley will join Citi one day, maybe when Ivanov's non-solicit expires sometime in late 2027? This is not confirmed, though.
Luisa Leyenaar-Huntingford </news/luisa-leyenaar-huntingford>, Citi's former co-head of global infrastructure banking, based in London, left in April, shortly before Vlad arrived. Citi hired her from Goldman in 2022. Her whereabouts are unknown.

item.title: Some people at hedge fund Tudor are having a wonderful time in London. Not all
item.description:
Macro hedge funds </news/2021/05/how-to-get-a-job-in-a-global-macro-fund> had a good 2025. – The top five performing funds in 2025 were macro funds, according to Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-01-02/bridgewater-d-e-shaw-among-biggest-hedge-fund-gainers-in-2025>. One macro fund, however, had a more mixed year.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Accounts have just been released for Tudor Capital Europe LLP, the main UK subsidiary of US hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> Tudor Investment Corporation. They cover the year ending 31 March.
Tudor’s London business had a good year. Revenue rose by 31%, employee count by 30%, and average pay per head by 12%. It’s the seventh consecutive year of headcount growth for the firm, at least, and the third consecutive year of growth for revenue and pay.
Tudor's 153 London employees earned an average of $416k each, up from the 118 people earning $373k on average in 2025. Back in 2019, 64 Tudor employees in London earned $256k on average.
Surprisingly, pay for the fund’s members - UK legal jargon for partners in a partnership – was down. Tudor’s portfolio managers (as most members are) enjoyed compensation of only $8.0m per head in the year ending March 2026 - down by 6% from 2025. The number of members was flat at 10 on the previous year.
Tudor’s reporting period overlaps very well with Stuart Riley’s </news/stuart-riley> presence at the firm. Riley was head of London rates trading for Goldman Sachs and a co-founder of macro fund Rokos Capital Management. Having joined Tudor in February 2025, he left less than a year and a half later for fellow hedge fund ARP Global Capital </news/stuart-riley> in Dubai.

item.title: Citi's longserving head of fintech banking in EMEA resigned
item.description:
As we have reported often, Citi has been hiring senior bankers. </news/as-citi-and-jp-morgan-swap-staff-people-are-wondering-who-will-be-next>But it has also been losing senior bankers, often to JPMorgan.
Mark Tweedie, a senior banker at Citi is understood to have resigned. We do not know where he is going, but maybe it is to JPMorgan too.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Tweedie was Citi's head of fintech banking for EMEA, based out of London. He joined the bank in 1999 and he had worked there for nearly 28 years. It is conceivable that he is simply retiring.
Tweedie declined to comment on his whereabouts. Citi declined to comment on what Tweedie is doing.
Fortunately, Citi has amassed a deep bench of technology bankers who can help fill Tweedie's experienced shoes. They include Amit Nayyar who was previously head of fintech banking at JPMorgan and who joined Citi last year. At the time, </news/now-citi-hired-jp-morgan-s-head-of-emea-fintech-banking>we thought Nayyar would be Tweedie's co-head and wondered how Tweedie might feel about sharing his job. In fact, Nayyar was given a bigger role as co-head of all EMEA technology investment banking and so was presumably Tweedie's boss.

item.title: Morning Coffee: JPMorgan decides to get tough with Jane Street. Former hedge fund manager and BoA banker might be the next Jamie Dimon
item.description:
Investment banks </news/what-is-an-investment-bank> often have a funny kind of “frenemies” relationship with that part of their client base which consists of other financial institutions. It is possible to make a lot of money out of dealing with them, but there is often quite a lot of overlap between the clients’ business, and things which the bank would like to make money out of itself. This tension has to be managed quite carefully; in prime brokerage, financial sponsors </news/financial-sponsors-bankers-2026>and several other areas, the banks want to help their clients do well, but maybe not to do too well.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
An important recent example of this might be the growth of market making firms like Citadel Securities </news/2022/10/how-to-get-a-job-at-citadel>and of proprietary trading firms like Jane Street <https://www.ft.com/content/07e849ac-ea87-4227-81d4-7f18b0d7d473?syn-25a6b1a6=1>. In a short period of time, they went from useful counterparties, to being serious competitors, to taking dominant share in a corner of the market (cash equities trading) which the banks had previously considered their own. So when Jane Street started to move into fixed income, this understandably raised concerns.
The Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/07e849ac-ea87-4227-81d4-7f18b0d7d473?syn-25a6b1a6=1> is reporting that JPMorgan (and possibly other banks – nobody is willing to talk on the record) has significantly reduced the amount of lending that it is prepared to extend to Jane Street, and to other market making firms like Citadel Securities. There might be all sorts of reasons for that, but it is noticeable that the move came shortly after Jane Street began to offer quotes in US Treasuries, and after Citadel Securities poached JPMorgan's head of high touch trading </news/jpmorgan-citadel-securities>and then Jamie Dimon mentioned the firm as a significant competitor in his shareholder letter.
“People familiar with the situation” suggest that there had been “internal tensions” at JPM, with the trading desks getting unhappy that other parts of the bank were financing an attempt to eat their lunch. Since JPM apparently provided about 5% of Jane Street’s total leverage, it’s hard to say that this was the only thing going on, but they might have had a point.
Under Jamie Dimon, JP Morgan has made something of a habit of being the first of the bulge bracket to stand up and defend the franchise against client-competitors. He led the way, for example, in putting an end to the practice of “on cycle recruiting <https://www.ft.com/content/cca6a7f9-2319-4a57-b6e5-800e6f5aff6d?syn-25a6b1a6=1>”, whereby private equity firms effectively used the sell side as a free training program for their analysts. At the time, this was seen as a courageous move, which might have damaged JPM’s relationship with the important and lucrative financial sponsors client base.
If the rest of the Street follows JPM’s lead, then although the proprietary trading firms are unlikely to go away entirely, they might at least be slowed down in their growth. Sometimes the most important role of a market leader is to provide leadership.
Elsewhere, when Jamie Dimon finally retires and the definitive biography of his career is written, one of the most important chapters will detail how he built his reputation as a loyal lieutenant (of Sandy Weill), and then cemented it after leaving to turn around a troubled bank (Bank One). It’s quite a story. And even more interestingly, it’s one which appears to be repeating itself, as Mike Lyons takes over the CEO role at Truist <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-31/moynihan-protege-gets-shot-at-fixing-dead-money-bank-truist>.
Lyons started his career at Fleet Bank, on the strategy team of its then CEO, Brian Moynihan. After leaving that job to join Morgan Stanley, and then spending some time as a hedge fund manager at Maverick Capital, he returned to work with Moynihan as head of corporate strategy at Bank of America. He left BoA in 2011 to help build PNC Bank into a midwestern powerhouse.
And now he is being given his first major banking CEO role, at Truist, the biggest bank in the Southeast USA, but a perennial underperformer that needs a bit of firm management after two previous “decisively nice” leaders. If the story continues in the same way, we should probably expect to see him coming back to Wall Street in triumph some time around 2030.
Meanwhile …
There is a lot of coming and going in the FX derivatives market; HSBC have hired Pierre Viandaz, formerly an MD at Goldman Sachs. Goldman also recently lost Andrei Kazantsev to Citigroup, but have hired Simon Costello from Balyasny. (Financial News <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/hsbc-hires-goldman-sachs-trader-in-fx-push-1970a0ef?mod=topic_news>)
It’s not particularly common for portfolio managers to leave Bluecrest, but Ben Atlas did it last year. As his non-compete comes to an end, he will be managing $1bn for ExodusPoint, who are also allowing him to give his pod the undeniably cool name of “Atlas Capital”. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-02/ex-bluecrest-trader-to-run-1-billion-macro-pod-at-exoduspoint?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=260902&utm_campaign=author_19458291>)
“If the number of hours they’re working on a matter has come down because of AI . . . our expectation is for costs to come down significantly per transaction”. Banks are asking law firms to pass on some of the savings, and presumably hoping that cllients don’t start thinking in a similar way about the bankers’ fees. (FT <https://www.ft.com/content/5240a6ac-b2e8-4897-a0a4-cbc7fc283bc9?syn-25a6b1a6=1>)
The “millionaire factory” at Macquarie wants to open a new production line in metals trading. As well as hiring, it is also looking to acquire physical metal trading firms. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-01/macquarie-eyes-trader-acquisitions-as-it-seeks-growth-in-metals>)
According to various sellers of creatine-enhanced smoothies and “nutrition brands”, bankers are looking to funny tasting drinks full of mushrooms and yerba mate, to give them a “competitive edge” (FT <https://www.ft.com/content/81515570-62ab-4f45-a526-04b1c715c160>)
For any junior bankers who want a career change and feel like they might be good with a pair of pliers, the labour shortage for Australian data centres is so acute that they are offering A$200,000 (US$143,000) for junior electricians. (AFR <https://www.afr.com/technology/the-new-megatrend-that-s-created-the-200-000-junior-sparkie-20260831-p60sxb>)
If you’ve been working on a structured finance deal in the renewable energy sector, and can’t help thinking you recognise one of the bankers from Excelsior Capital Partners, it’s because he used to play Nick Moore in the hit 80s comedy “Family Ties”. (Parade <https://parade.com/celebrities/41-years-after-debuting-on-family-ties-as-mallorys-boyfriend-nick-scott-valentine-is-unrecognizable-at-68>)

item.title: Maybe Jain Global's portfolio managers are just incredibly talented
item.description:
Hedge fund Jain Global has had a few changes of plan. Initially, it was maybe going to launch with $8-10bn. <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2024-01-18/jain-global-slashes-target-to-as-low-as-5-billion-before-debut>Actually, it raised $5.3bn. Initially, it was going to be a standalone new multistrategy hedge fund with its own set of investors. Actually, it's in the process of returning money to investors by the end of this month and will thereafter run money entirely for Millennium.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
What Jain Global has been consistent about, is its desire to hire really very good portfolio managers. Speaking earlier this year </news/as-jain-global-p-ms-take-headhunter-calls-bobby-jain-explains-why-they-need-patience>, Bobby Jain, who founded Jain Global, said his modus operandi was to hire a mix of steady performers and "35-year-old-killers" and to take 'good people and make them great.'
Seven months later, Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-01/jain-s-hedge-fund-made-1-8-billion-as-millennium-cash-rolls-in>says Jain Global has 400 employees in total and 65 portfolio managers. Maybe these portfolio managers are very great indeed, because Bloomberg also said that the gross returns on "called capital" (capital actually invested and received by Jain Global) were 41% since the fund's debut in July 2024.
This sounds impressive, and also like every investor might like to shower some money upon Jain Global in light of Bobby Jain's talent-spotting abilities.
However, gross returns are not net returns. Gross returns don't include costs like technology, offices, or paying Jain Global's talented portfolio managers themselves. When these costs are included, Jain Global's net returns withered to 8.4% over the same period, comprised of 0.5% in 2024 (from July onwards), of 3.7% last year and of 4% so far in 2026.
Costs therefore might be an issue. Jain Global declined to comment for this article. One insider with knowledge of other funds said costs elsewhere are typically around 10% of assets under management.
Not all of Jain Global's assets were initially called up to be managed. Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-01-15/jain-hedge-fund-costs-cut-into-750-million-profits-last-year>reported in January that Jain Global began 2025 with only $2bn deployed. It said that Jain Global ended last year with $5bn invested. The total $5.3bn was only fully invested 20 months after launch (ie. around March 2026).
The delay in calling up Jain's capital seems to be down to a delay in finding enough great portfolio managers. Bloomberg said yesterday that it took a long time for Jain to "recruit trading talent."
While trading talent proved elusive, Jain Global had front-loaded its costs. Speaking in February, Bobby Jain said front-loaded costs were part of the plan. "One of the things my dad said is 'take the pain upfront,'" he declared. "It's not chicken and egg, it's 'just chicken'," he added. "You have to build it all off your own balance sheet and then the money comes in....I was prepared for all that."
Taking the pain upfront meant that while Jain's talented portfolio managers generated $750m in trading profits last year, Bloomberg reported that investors only received $190m of that after fees and expenses. The money was supposed to flow through to investors in time. "You're going to see the operating leverage start kicking in," Jain also said seven months ago.
The operating leverage will hopefully start kicking in for Millennium. In the meantime, Bloomberg reports that Jain Global is still hiring and is pitching itself to very talented PMs as "a trading firm where portfolio managers collaborate with one another, whereas Millennium provides more independence and autonomy." Jon Stead </news/hedge-fund-jain-global-hired-morgan-stanley-s-head-of-high-yield-trading-in-london>, the ex-head of high yield trading at Morgan Stanley, appears to be in agreement with this and is joining Jain Global soon.
Given the $1.8bn of gross trading profits generated since launch, Jain Global's current total of 65 portfolio managers has generated an average of $28m each in profits over the past two years or so. However, not all of them were employed from inception and so actual profits per PM are likely to be far higher. If Bobby Jain ever retires from running Jain Global, he could probably work in business development instead. </news/hedge-fund-business-development-executive-bde>

item.title: Citi already made three rounds of job cuts in New York City this year
item.description:
Citi employs a lot more people </news/citi-has-quietly-cut-7-000-jobs-this-year-what-about-the-other-9-000>than in the old days and it is not averse to getting rid of some of them. Some members of Citi data teams </news/citi-is-making-cuts-to-its-data-teams-they-may-be-substantial-or-not>were quietly cut in July. It turns out there were cuts across the business in April and in February too.
Recently filed WARN (worker adjustment and retaining notifications) for Citi's New York business show the bank making a total of 820 cuts at Citibank so far this year, 58 cuts at Citigroup global markets and three cuts at Citigroup technology.
However, the cuts were not made all at once. At Citibank's 388 Greenwich Street office, where most of the cuts were made, 248 people were cut in February, 304 were cut in April and another 268 were cut in July.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Similarly, at Citigroup Global Markets 16 were cut in February, 30 were cut in April and 12 were cut in July. At Citigroup Technology, one person was cut on each occasion.
A spokesperson for the bank said they were grateful for the work of those leaving and that: "These changes reflect adjustments we’re making to ensure our staffing levels, locations and expertise align with current business needs; efficiencies we have gained through technology; and progress against our Transformation work, which is nearing Citi’s target state."
Citi CEO Jane Fraser said in April </news/citi-has-quietly-cut-7-000-jobs-this-year-what-about-the-other-9-000>that 90% of the transformation work on Citi's 2020 consent order was done. She added in July that Citi was already largely operating at its "target state." Citi hired Tricia Kissinger </news/citi-hired-md-from-regulator>from the Federal Reserve (which imposed the consent order) as a managing director helping with its regulatory relationships in August.
Before the consent order was in place, Citi employed 210,000 people. Following the consent order, it added 30,000 people to help shape up areas like regulatory reporting. Speaking in May, Citi CFO Gonzalo Luchetti <https://www.citigroup.com/rcs/citigpa/storage/public/investor-day/citi-ID26-financial-overview-presentation.pdf>, said the bank would be cutting temporary costs relating to its transformation. It's also automating roles with AI. Either way, people are dripping out in New York. At the same time, though, Citi has been hiring </news/as-citi-and-jp-morgan-swap-staff-people-are-wondering-who-will-be-next> senior bankers from the likes of JPMorgan and Deutsche Bank.

item.title: How to get a job in venture capital
item.description:
Venture Capital (VC) firms invest in new and fast-growing start-ups. The culture in VC firms is more relaxed and less corporate than traditional private equity jobs. Compensation is also lower compared to private equity. VC firms can pay carried interest, but it's not common. Exit opportunities take a long time to achieve, and most start-ups fail.
Technically speaking, venture capital is a subset of private equity </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-private-equity>: like big private equity (PE) firms, venture capital firms invest in companies that aren't publicly traded on a stock exchange. But working for a VC firm is a wildly different experience to a career in the likes of Blackstone </news/blackstone-pay-london> or Carlyle. </news/pay-carlyle-private-equity>
Follow eFinancialCareers on Google News here. <https://news.google.com/publications/CAAqMggKIixDQklTR3dnTWFoY0tGV1ZtYVc1aGJtTnBZV3hqWVhKbFpYSnpMbU52YlNnQVAB?ceid=GB:en&oc=3>
What is venture capital?
Venture capital firms traditionally invest in early-stage companies, taking a minor ownership stake alongside various other investors. Traditional PE firms, by contrast, tend to invest in more mature companies, and take majority stakes in their portfolio companies. PE firms tend to have more specialisation, at least on a fund-by-fund basis, while VCs are more generalist.
The biggest difference between VCs and PE firms, though, is the level of support they claim to provide for founders. Luke Pappas, partner at New Enterprise Associates, said at the 2026 LSE Alternative Investments Conference (AIC) in February that VC is all about "look[ing] for the secret sauce in the founding team" and having "conviction that this team is going to be the one to change things." That conviction is necessary because "all the companies we're interested in are inherently unprofitable for the first few years." The involvement of VCs isn't always a good thing in the eyes of the founders; Joel Perlman, co-founder of fintech </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-fintech> OakNorth Bank, said at a conference in 2024 </news/oak-north-founder-my-exit-strategy-is-a-clean-heart-attack-at-my-desk> that founders often "drink the kool aid" and "mess up their company" by following too many demands from their VCs.
Some VCs are much more involved than others. The likes of Y Combinator are classed as start-up incubators; they have a more direct role in the running of start-ups, to the point where they may even match potential founders together.
VCs have a reputation for inflating the valuations of their portfolio companies. Pappas said "many of my hedge fund </news/all-the-jobs-in-hedge-funds> friends and private equity </news/private-equity-job-titles>friends will ping me and tell me that we're not very rational in our pricing." He said that many of the best investments in VC are blink-and-you'll-miss-it, however, and that accepting an inflated valuation is necessary; "if this company ultimately becomes a $10bn company in the long run, it won't matter much."
Fundraising in VC isn't what it used to be, however. A report <https://carta.com/data/resources/state-of-startups-2025/> from accounting infrastructure firm Carta estimated that there was a total of $110bn in start-up investments through its platform last year, down from a high of $220.3bn in 2021. The Wall Street Journal <https://www.wsj.com/finance/investing/u-s-venture-capital-fundraising-falls-35-as-firms-stay-private-longer-601d6629?gaa_at=eafs&gaa_n=AWEtsqcmJtMGn0708IAAmI57STH_eJb-ZpWCi2dm2FEv_voBf6NEOr6LmFjk3u3X87w%3D&gaa_ts=698b69de&gaa_sig=ALXM_v5jL_2zYlZQYKuVxfcSXddtxZ2L-MRAnKSn21V__rbOS6mYZkhHRON4aBo2_63ubQv_vi3c6UbTgj-ZZA%3D%3D> reported in January that fundraising for US VC firms in 2025 was the lowest it had been for six years. Funds have a lot less margin for error, which is putting increased pressure on VC professionals.
What do you do in venture capital?
"VCs are not glamorous," said Antler partner Hannah Leach at the AIC. "It's honestly a lot of admin." You'll be sitting in numerous meetings for your portfolio companies and researching new ones. Leach said "you need to be adept at sending a cold email </news/finance/cold-email-investment-banking-job>" if you want to win new business.
Your job is to see through the noise in the start-up world. Pappas said that "every day, I open up my news app and see 15 different products that people say are changing the world." Leach said that VC is all about doing your homework and "go[ing] into conversations well-informed regardless of asset class."
Cherry Ventures principal Nadja Reischel said that you have to look for "founders who are super obsessed with the product," as that obsession will carry them through the next ten years of working in their start-up. You'll also need to gauge their learning speed and commercial instinct; "you want people who are talking to not 20 but 2,000 potential customers," Reischel said.
All of this typically translates to long hours. Leach said that "work-life balance doesn't quite exist in VC... you need to want to get up at 7am and work through to midnight." Reischel said that "venture is pretty much 24/7" and suggested that she hasn't taken a Sunday off since she joined her firm.
There are many more stories of failure in VC than success. Using the UK fintech scene as an example, market intelligence platform Tracxn said there have been 18,000 fintech start-ups created in the UK to date, of which just 30 have become unicorns (start-ups valued at $1bn+) and almost 6,000 have become defunct. The goal of VC is to cast a wide net and invest across a range of start-ups expecting those few unicorns to make up for the losses made on the failures.
What skills and experience are VC firms looking for?
To succeed in VC, you need to be a people person, but there's more to it than that.
Pappas said that you're a good fit for VC if your "brain likes to context switch a lot of times," as you'll be working across a wide range of products and teams. Leach said you also "need to be good at psychology."
Shayan Roy Chowdhury, MD of VC education platform, the Newton Venture Program, told members of our community, The Bubble, <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/t/ama-im-the-managing-director-of-newton-venture-program-a-vc-education-program/4767> that the most important skills are "critical thinking, ability to think big, relationship building, time management, and clarity of communication." An investor at one UK-focused VC firm said in The Bubble <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/t/ama-im-a-vc-investor/5330/14>that there is much less reliance on "'traditional’ valuation methodologies" in VC compared to private equity but you'll need to be a good judge of character as you're "taking a position on the people involved to be able to deliver."
The investor said that there are three broad types of profile VCs hire for 'operating principal' roles, the people that get involved in the day to day running of portfolio companies. They hire subject-matter experts for specific sectors who have their "finger on the pulse and are often at the forefront of emerging trends." They also hire "proven operators," who have worked in start-ups and have experience scaling them. These are often ex-founders, chief operating officers (COOs) or chief revenue officers (CROs). The other profile of operating principal is a "functional specialist" in an area like hiring, go-to-market (GTM) or AI who can assist that function across multiple portfolio companies at once. Hires can be one, or multiple, of these archetypes.
As with their founders, VC firms also want their employees to be passionate. Pappas said that, if you're not, "there's going to be 1,000 people who are genuinely interested and they will outperform you." Leach said that demonstrating your passion is particularly hard as a graduate, but suggested building a "shadow portfolio of companies you think will do very well" to stand out.
Having a financial background isn't always necessary. Speaking at the AIC in 2024, LocalGlobe partner Mish Mashkautsan said "template paths" like banking or consulting </news/pay-mckinsey-bain-bcg-big-four> are "uninspiring" as routes into VC. Instead, he said "the best thing you can do is take a bet on yourself." Chowdhury said in The Bubble that many people join VCs after working in a start-up in a role like a founder's associate </news/the-most-exciting-and-bizarre-job-for-24-year-olds-at-revolut-and-other-fintechs> or chief of staff, while the UK investor said that VC is "somewhat more accepting of non-traditional profiles, especially at earlier stages." One ex-banker in VC previously told us </news/2020/11/how-to-move-out-of-banking-and-into-venture-capital> that big name brands are much more important for getting a VC job in Europe than they are in America.
What jobs are available in VC?
Unlike PE, most venture capital firms do not have robust intern or graduate recruitment programs. There are exceptions, like Bessemer Ventures' analyst program, but you'll likely have to monitor the recruiting pages of the firms you're interested in.
There aren't that many VC jobs available, even at the top firms. Andreessen Horowitz, for example, is one of the largest firms but only has 16 current openings. Y Combinator, another major VC, has just six openings. Sequoia Capital has no current openings. Roles in VC are extremely oversubscribed, so you'll need to rely on connections where possible. If you're a right fit for the people-centric world of VC, that shouldn't be hard.
How is AI changing venture capital?
AI is having a profound impact on VC firms by virtue of the fact that almost every start-up today is now an AI firm in some way shape or form. The technology has provided some huge opportunities, like the chance to invest in burgeoning AI labs, but this often comes with chaos.
The biggest AI firms have grown at an unprecedented rate; Anthropic, for example, was valued at $4.1bn in 2023, but has since grown its valuation to almost one trillion dollars. The growth of AI technologies has also made it easier than ever to build a start-up, meaning that there are many more companies for VCs to invest in, and a lot more work to decide which are worth the money.
One of the biggest spanners in the works for VCs today is the growth of 'reverse acqui-hires,' in which companies pay huge amounts of money to sign the most important people from a growing start-up without buying the company itself. Roxanne Varza, director of start-up campus Station F, said at the Sifted Summit last year that many founders "aren't even thinking of an exit strategy," and are treating their start-up as an audition so that they'll be picked up by one of the AI giants. If they get hired, the VCs that invested in them could be left with a worthless company if they don't manage the crisis effectively.
While some of the biggest companies are planning IPOs to give their investors liquidity, it's much more common to operate in the secondaries market, in which stakes in companies are sold from one private investor to another. Delta-v Capital partner Garrett Marsilio told the Journal <https://www.wsj.com/articles/venture-capitalists-predict-many-ai-startups-will-get-weeded-out-in-2026-61134d89>there are "trillions of dollars trapped inside private technology companies,” and that there will be an "explosion" of activity in the secondaries market as people try to cash out (or in).
All of this means that the pressure on VC investors to see through the noise and invest in viable, healthy companies is more important than ever. They're increasingly using AI on a daily basis to do that. A survey <https://www.affinity.co/report/affinity-predictions-report?preview=affinity-preview-2026>from private capital CRM firm Affinity found that 85% of dealmakers use AI to automate daily tasks in 2026, up from 76% last year. It's primarily used to assist in research tasks for companies given the ability of large language models (LLMs) to process complex documents quickly. 28% of respondents said they also used AI to make investment decisions, up from 13% in 2025.
How much do VC jobs pay?
A 2026 salary survey <https://www.newcomer.co/p/heres-what-your-fellow-venture-capitalists?utm_source=substack&publication_id=82416&post_id=186864407&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share> from Venture5 found that analysts in VC earn $80k on average. You'll earn $130k-150k as an associate, ~$200k as a mid-level professional, </news/2023/01/venture-capitalism-jobs> then over $300k on average if you can make partner.
A key appeal of working in PE (and thus VC) is the opportunity to earn carried interest, </news/what-is-carried-interest> which is a percentage of the profits should a portfolio company have a large enough exit. Only 24% of VC analysts reported that they earned carry, however.
As a partner, pay depends on how large your fund is. The survey found that partners at VC funds with more than $500m in assets under management (AUM) earned $585k in total compensation. When AUM was $250-500m, average compensation was $402k.
Have a confidential story, tip, or comment you’d like to share? Contact: +44 7537 182250 (SMS, WhatsApp or voicemail). Telegram: @SarahButcher. Click here to fill in our anonymous form </about/editor-tips>, or email editortips@efinancialcareers.com. Signal also available.
Bear with us if you leave a comment at the bottom of this article: all our comments are moderated by human beings. Sometimes these humans might be asleep, or away from their desks, so it may take a while for your comment to appear. Eventually it will – unless it’s offensive or libelous (in which case it won’t.)

A 2026 salary survey <https://www.newcomer.co/p/heres-what-your-fellow-venture-capitalists?utm_source=substack&publication_id=82416&post_id=186864407&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share> from Venture5 found that analysts in VC earn $80k on average. You'll earn $130k-150k as an associate, ~$200k as a mid-level professional, </news/2023/01/venture-capitalism-jobs> then over $300k on average if you can make partner.
A key appeal of working in PE (and thus VC) is the opportunity to earn carried interest, </news/what-is-carried-interest> which is a percentage of the profits should a portfolio company have a large enough exit. Only 24% of VC analysts reported that they earned carry, however.
As a partner, pay depends on how large your fund is. The survey found that partners at VC funds with more than $500m in assets under management (AUM) earned $585k in total compensation. When AUM was $250-500m, average compensation was $402k.
