item.title: What does a private equity associate actually do?
item.description:
Private equity </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-private-equity> (PE) associates are the first proper rung on the industry’s ladder. Most PE associates arrive after two or three years of an analyst program </news/banks-weird-hierarchies-analysts-associates-vps-mds> in an investment bank, or maybe sooner. What does their new job involve?
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Private equity associates spend their time on two key things. They are responsible for both looking for new businesses for the fund to invest in, and for keeping an eye on how businesses the fund has already invested in are getting on. Adis, a principal at Blackstone, told us she </news/2022/06/day-in-the-life-private-equity-blackstone> spent her days as an associate taking expert calls with professionals in the industries she covers, drafting models and assembling investment materials just like a junior M&A </news/get-a-job-in-ma> banker would, and leading a team of analysts producing their own work.
When we spoke to David </news/private-equity-day-in-the-life>, an associate in KKR's technology, media and telecoms (TMT) team in New York, his day began with analytical work – thesis building and diligence, often alongside colleagues on the European team. In the afternoon he ran a diligence session, putting questions to the team working on an acquisition and playing back what the data showed in KKR's models. Associates, he said, get a lot of responsibility to guide the direction of those sessions.
This is the first key distinction between the role of a private equity associate and that of an M&A junior </news/what-are-ma-jobs>. An M&A analyst produces analysis to support a client's decision – an associate produces analysis to help inform the investment decisions of the private equity firm he or she works for.
When you work in private equity, your responsibility escalates fast. When David returns to analytical work later in the day, he doesn't just build operating models, he also chooses how to appraise the businesses he's investigating. He decides which analyses of the diligence data will answer the key questions, and he frames how his work is presented to the deal team and the investment committee that make the final investment decision.
AI is changing this process </news/ai-changing-private-equity>. More of the groundwork is automated. For example, Blackstone's chief technology officer John Stecher said in May <https://www.blackstone.com/insights/article/ai-at-scale-a-conversation-with-blackstones-cto-and-global-head-of-the-operating-team/> that reviewing the thousands of documents attached to a deal used to be a weekend-long activity and can now be done in minutes, and that the firm's private equity teams are using targeted tools to move faster from raw deal documents to financial models.

item.title: Morning Coffee: The man with the hardest job at Citi fired 20% of his team & is hiring a new one. Stop negotiating your base salary, start negotiating your bonus
item.description:
Andy Sieg </news/andy-sieg-women> is an important guy at Citi. Hired personally by Citi CEO Jane Fraser </news/jane-fraser-citi-sexism>, who drove to his home to persuade him onboard, he is tasked with growing Citi's wealth business. As of last November </news/andy-sieg-wealth-citi>, he is also tasked with heading its US retail bank. Sieg is a man with broad shoulders.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
He is also a man unafraid to fire people and to hire some new ones. In a profile of Sieg and of Citi's wealth business, Financial News <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/the-battle-to-revitalise-citigroups-wealth-unit-ca61df71?mod=homepage>notes that by his own admission at Citi's May's investor day </news/citi-investor-day-2026>, Sieg has fired 20% of people in Citi's wealth business since he arrived in late 2023. Various senior people have left, possibly of their own accords. But Sieg is busy hiring some new ones in.
For a man accused (and exonerated </news/andy-sieg-citi-investigation>following an investigation from Citi's preferred law firm) by Citi MDs of harsh behaviour towards women on his team, Sieg has hired a lot of new women in. He has always denied the allegations, as has Fraser herself. Following the exits of women like Ida Liu </news/andy-sieg-investigation>(now at HSBC), Naz Vahid, </news/andy-sieg-citi-complaints-exits> Dina Saada and Julia Carreon </news/citi-andy-sieg-case>from senior roles, Financial News notes that Sieg has hired the likes of Dawn Nordberg from Morgan Stanley to run integrated client solutions, Kate Moore from BlackRock as chief investment officer for Citi Wealth and Anne McCosker from Goldman Sachs as global head of lending.
More hires are to come. As Sieg endeavours to achieve a target 20% return on tangible equity in its wealth unit (up from 7% last year and -2% when he arrived in 2023) and to grow revenues by 10%, the intention is to hire 100 private bankers and investment counsellors by 2028. James Holder, the head of Citi's private bank for the UK, Europe, Middle East and Africa, who tells FN that he interacts with Sieg most days, says the new hiring could be on his patch. The Middle East is a priority; continental Europe has potential. A headhunter tells FN that it's cheaper to hire in Europe, but that all this recruitment will cost Citi a lot of money.
Sieg will need to juice his newly refreshed team. Holder suggests Sieg's very good at this and says his "very direct and personal engagement with the business” is great. Sieg came from Merrill Lynch where the culture was "highly competitive, highly performance-driven," notes the headhunter. Sieg is instilling a bit of this sparkle at Citi. He's also reportedly focused on asset gathering, rather than revenues.
Good things are happening. FN notes that the return on equity in Citi's wealth business is now above the RoE in its markets business and that client assets rose 14% year-on-year in the second quarter (and, coincidentally, in many previous quarters).
But people are still leaving. FN says global head of wealth financial planning Jonathan Peterson and Canada head of investments Dale Powell have departed of late. Peterson joined from JPMorgan in 2022. Sieg's seat is not easy. Wells Fargo analyst Mike Mayo suggests his targets might be unattainable. “If Andy Sieg actually gets the financial targets that he has posted, you will have to change his name from Andy to Houdini,” he says. This will be an interesting transition.
Separately, if you are trying to get a quant job </news/quant-jobs-finance>with an electronic trading firm </news/difference-between-electronic-trading-firms>or hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> and you are negotiating your salary </news/how-much-do-electronic-trading-jobs-really-pay>, you are doing it wrong.
Substack YoungandCalculated <https://youngandcalculated.substack.com/p/the-comp-negotiation-nobody-teaches>notes that salaries are only 15% to 30% of what juniors typically earn. The rest is bonus. Salaries are typically between $150k and $250k for quant researchers </news/what-is-a-quant-researcher-hedge-fund> and can be difficult to negotiate because they are controlled by HR. YoungandCalculated says guaranteed bonuses are controlled by hiring managers and can be "negotiated in an afternoon."
Meanwhile...
Apollo, Blackstone, Brookfield, BlackRock, Goldman and KKR are working on a $500bn funding package for AI infrastructure development with NVIDIA. (Financial Times) <https://www.ft.com/content/98a8fd17-15b6-4f67-9cb4-825722b11348?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Hyperscalers already $1.5tn of lease commitments, of which about $1tn doesn’t appear in their financial statements because leases aren't stated until they're started. Once these contractual obligations come due, they will be considerable. (Financial Times) <. https://www.ft.com/content/a0a07cce-6d19-4b1e-a73b-9855a06ba7b3>
Private credit defaults are growing. So far, the bad loans are cropping up primarily in healthcare companies, like dental-service provider Affordable Care, or businesses affected by higher oil prices, including plastic-film maker Loparex. What if they spread to software companies, which make up 20% or more of the loans in many funds? (WSJ) < https://www.wsj.com/finance/investing/private-credit-is-under-growing-strain-despite-industrys-upbeat-tone-e5abf388?mod=hp_lead_pos1>
Mark Zuckerberg had long thoughts about AI: "We believe that delivering superintelligence to everyone is the way to answer this question. This follows the tradition of putting the power of supercomputers and the internet in everyone's pockets and on our desks. Rather than centralizing superintelligence, we should distribute it widely and give every person the ability to direct it." (Meta) <https://www.meta.com/thefutureisforeveryone/>
Zuckerberg thinks there will be a larger number of companies with fewer people” employed at each firm" and that “People also continually come up with new ideas to make our lives better and new jobs to bring those ideas to life.” (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-10/five-takeaways-from-zuckerberg-s-6-500-word-manifesto-on-ai?srnd=homepage-uk>
VARA, another hedge fund focused on AI investments, fell 44% in July. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-10/ai-focused-hedge-fund-vara-drops-44-in-july-on-stock-plunge>
Hong Kong bankers at Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan are working on the Shein IPO and it sounds complicated. Shein was valued at $100bn in 2022 but is now down to $30bn. US tariffs, shipping costs and competition from Temu have taken their toll, and Chinese investors are wary. (Financial Times) <https://www.ft.com/content/62d3a32d-8a38-4136-b32c-36f25099b91f?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
10 places are paying up to $100k a month for preferential access to the Tweets of Donald Trump on Truth Social. (WSJ) <https://www.wsj.com/business/media/trump-media-djt-2q-2026-earnings-report-stock-8118ee37>
PWC usually ends its US internship with a multiday trip to Disney World. Not any more. (Business Insider) <https://www.businessinsider.com/pwc-us-cancels-disney-world-intern-trip-2026-8>
Citi hired Jean-Baptiste Charlet from Morgan Stanley to lead its French business. (Financial News) <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/citigroup-hires-morgan-stanleys-charlet-to-lead-france-banking-team-14d7bb0c >
Women thrive in warm offices. (Atlantic) <https://www.theatlantic.com/health/archive/2019/05/warm-offices-women-productivity/589966/?taid=6a7a3f5ba8d1ba000141b3ad&utm_campaign=WigwamQuan&utm_content=edit-promo&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
A Citi employee says she was laid off by telephone whilst on vacation. (IBTimes) <https://www.ibtimes.co.uk/citigroups-ongoing-workforce-reductions-personal-account-1813222>
LinkedIn quashes more than 200,000 AI-generated spam comments every day before they go live. It also correctly detects an estimated 94% of generic, or AI-generated, posts, and doesn't distribute them. (WSJ) <https://www.wsj.com/cmo-today/linkedin-wants-users-to-lean-less-on-ai-maybe-a-lot-less-8e03b2aa>

item.title: It's hot. So are people who can help hedge funds predict the weather
item.description:
In case you haven't noticed, it's been a hot summer. Records are being broken, crops are being destroyed by drought and if you're a hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job>trying to see into the future, it's never been more important to employ someone who can tell you what this year's 'super el Niño' <https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-02293-y>might do next.
Step forward the quants and meteorologists who can forecast the weather and the traders who can monetise their predictions. They've been popular with hedge funds since at least 2018, when Citadel hired a team of 20 people from weather focused hedge fund Cumulus and started a trend. Since then, Citadel has gone deeper into the weather business and other funds have followed.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
In the past few months, there have been multiple hires in the space, both at Citadel and elsewhere. In July, Citadel recruited Russell Martin, a gas and power trading managing director (MD) from Goldman Sachs to trade weather derivatives in its Houston office. Point72 hired Alex Alifimoff as head of AI Weather in its commodities team in Stamford. Alifimoff will presumably be using AI to predict the weather rather than predicting the weather over data centres; he joined from Citadel where his LinkedIn account says he built AI weather models to support the commodity trading desk.
Rival funds have also been strengthening their weather teams. Balyasny Asset Management has had a weather team since at least 2021, when it hired Alexander Goldstein from Credit Suisse. Goldstein moved to Millennium in 2024 and now leads the weather analytics team there. BAM promoted London-based weather research Sean Moshe Nassimih to become its lead in weather research in June 2026.
Smaller hedge funds have been hiring too. Nanook Energy Advisors, which trades the European energy markets, hired Emmanuele Silvio Gentile from the National Centre for Atmospheric Science in Reading, UK, in June.
Thomas Carson, a director at headhunting firm Redstone Search <https://redstonesearch.com/>, said weather is likely to remain a hot topic for hiring. "The recent run of weather focused hires across major funds suggests the emergence of a new competitive frontier: proprietary weather intelligence as an alpha source, where outfits are treating weather as a cross asset alpha source rather than a niche commodity input," he informed us.
Not all meteorologists stay at hedge funds though. Nicholas Klingaman, Citadel's former head of weather, left in July 2025 and now describes himself as a "once and future weather guy." He was at Citadel for around four and half years. Maybe that's all that's needed to retire.

item.title: The skills you need for a career in private equity
item.description:
Do you want to work in private equity </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-private-equity>? It’s not for everyone. Even if the €37m+ ($43m+) historic paydays </news/private-equity-credit-pay> are appealing, you won’t be able to get your foot in the door without the right skillset. But what skillset is that exactly?
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
To start with, because private equity firms recruit overwhelmingly from investment banks </news/the-investment-banking-recruitment-process>, they expect to hire people who already have the standard banking skillset </news/skills-needed-m-a>: building financial models in Excel to value companies and pitchbooks in PowerPoint to win deals, as well as an exceptional capacity to work. But these are increasingly just table stakes, rather than the standout things that get you the job.
What funds actually want is an all-rounder; someone with insightful thinking and the ability to build relationships. "Private equity professionals need to be confident and persuasive, but also hard-edged when it comes to negotiating. They sell with their eyes and mouths and buy with their brains," said Gail McManus </news/top-private-equity-recruiter>, founder and former managing director of Private Equity Recruitment (PER). In this new world, where AI can build financial models and pitchbooks, she says </news/top-private-equity-recruiter> personality is even more important.
Private equity funds are looking for "Action Man or Action Woman," said McManus. You need to make things happen, to be "ultra-competitive, not let things stand in your way." And you need relationship skills alongside that: "it's all about winning the deal," McManus explained.
This doesn't make modelling skills redundant. In the US, private equity firms have developed a habit </news/jp-morgan-bankers-leave-for-private-equity> of hiring junior investment bankers early and sometimes before they've even joined banks, and they do so during one frenzied night of recruiting. UK firms do not do this, but assessment centres are still tough.
Juniors going through the private equity recruitment process are assessed on their financial modelling and on a case study, </news/private-equity-case-study-interview> which examines their judgement of what makes a good investment. Second to personality, it is good commercial judgement that is now the key differentiator in private equity recruitment, says McManus.
McManus says she likes to ask candidates, “if you were thinking of buying a coffee shop, what's the first thing you'd do?” If your answer is that you'd go and visit your local shop, to check whether the toilets are clean, count the customers, work out how many staff are on a shift and whether they look happy, then a career in private equity is probably for you. If your instinct is to go and find an analyst report on the coffee sector, you're probably better off working at an investment bank.
The point is not that research is bad. Research is good. It's that private equity is a business of owning things, and owners must form a view of how a company works, and not just what its numbers look like. You need to be interested in the mechanics of businesses rather than sitting behind a desk looking at spreadsheet (although there is an element of that too).
You also need to learn how to speak up. Being a private equity professional means being able to argue for or against a particular investment opportunity or sector in a room where people will push back. A passion for understanding the inner workings of business is essential, and so is the willingness to put a view on the table and be wrong in public.
In a world of high interest rates, understanding how a company operates and being able to improve it are increasingly important. A report from consulting firm Bain & Co, <https://www.bain.com/insights/welcome-to-a-new-era-global-private-equity-report-2026/>written in February 2026, noted that when private equity firms inveted in companies in 2015, they typically borrowed 50% of the purchase price at an interest rate of 6-7%. When investments were financed like this, Bain said the companies being purchased needed to generate 5% annual growth in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) over a five year period. This way, they would generate the 2.5x multiple on invested capital which private equity firms aim for when the company was sold five years later.
The world is very different when rates are 8-9%. At this interest rate, Bain said firms need to generate 10-12% annual growth in EBITDA to generate the 2.5x multiple they want.
Achieving 10-12% growth is not easy. To generate that kind of profit growth, a company needs to have falling costs and rising revenues, or both. And this means that the private equity firm which has bought the company needs to really understand how it works.
Because of this, private equity firms also increasingly need operational expertise. - People who can improve the firms they've invested in.
Recruitment consultancy DRAX summarised <https://draxexecutive.com/private-equity-outlook-2026-why-talent-will-define-the-next-cycle/> the newly desirable 'operational profile' for private equity firms in March 2026 as comprising, “commercial judgement with advanced analytical skills, people who can underwrite more accurately, pressure-test assumptions rigorously, navigate ambiguity, whilst having good ‘grit’ to go the extra mile.”
Alongside this, private equity firms are also increasingly interested in technological and data skills as AI permeates the industry </news/ai-changing-private-equity>. Apollo is hiring <https://www.dice.com/job-detail/a1f51e9b-2aa9-42a8-be5a-dfc4f2bcd744> for an “AI solutions and quantitative strategist” associate role, for example, that sits between its hybrid investments team and its quant team, ensuring that AI initiatives are “practical, high-impact and embedded into day-to-day workflows.”
You do not need to be a crack software engineer, but you do need to be versed on what these tools can and can't do. The majority of private equity firms expect AI to have a “material impact” on their portfolio companies in 2026, Bain reported this year <https://www.bain.com/insights/private-equitys-reality-check-gp-outlook-2026/>, with cost savings and revenue growth the most likely culprits. You need to be familiar with AI – we wrote more about that specifically here </news/ai-changing-private-equity>.

item.title: JPMorgan's top non-linear rates trader has left the bank
item.description:

JPMorgan declined to comment on Mernissi's whereabouts. Mernissi ignored our invitations to disclose his intentions.

item.title: "I am a junior investment banker. When I am not working, I am looking for a different job"
item.description:
I am a junior investment banker </news/what-is-an-investment-bank>working in the technology </news/technology-bankers>, media and telecommunications team (TMT) at a European bank in London. I read this article </news/technology-bankers>about the difficult life of a TMT banker and I suspect it was written by one of my colleagues.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Life here is tough. The culture at the bank I work for leaves a lot to be desired. Maybe this is the case at all European investment banks. People don't stay in this team. No one seems inclined to stay more than two years and many people leave after one.
I want to leave too. I spend most of my time working but during the times that I'm not working, I'm looking for other opportunities. It's a gruelling existence and leaves me with little time to myself.
It seems strange that the bank is unwilling to examine the reasons for all the departures. The problem here lies in the way that certain senior bankers manage the team and the effect that this has on junior staff. This is why juniors keep leaving. Management and HR are very aware that there are retention issues, but seem unbothered. Instead of examining the problem, they just keep hiring more managing directors (MDs) and vice presidents (VPs). </news/banks-weird-hierarchies-analysts-associates-vps-mds>
This will become a problem. At some point, they will not have enough good juniors to do the work. Maybe they think that AI will compensate </news/ai-in-ma-banking>.
For now, people continue to vote with their feet. I can only hope my next employer will be rather better and that it's not like this everywhere in banking.
Elias Pennington is a pseudonym

item.title: 29-year-old equity derivative VPs are being hired on large packages
item.description:
This is a good time to work in equity derivatives. Equities sales and trading </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank>revenues are booming and equity derivatives revenues are booming most of all. They were "exceptionally strong" in the first half of the year in the estimation of market intelligence firm Tricumen. </news/best-investment-banks-world>Speaking to CNBC <https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/01/goldman-traders-are-on-pace-for-a-record-year-a-close-up-look-at-how-theyre-doing-it.html> last week, Kevin Kelly, the global co-head of equities at Goldman Sachs, said volatility around single name stocks, combined with market appreciation, is generating demand for hedging: "The equity market generally has behaved as there’s AI winners and AI losers, and there was nothing in between."
In the circumstances, equity derivatives professionals are suddenly desirable, particularly at vice president (VP) level as banks build out their teams.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Headhunters and market participants say there's a comparative shortage of VP talent in the equity derivatives market. "There are limited candidates at VP level as a fair few have gone to hedge funds </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job>," says Marcus Newman, partner at search firm Omerta Group, <https://omerta-group.com/> a Kingsley Gate Company. "In turn, this has inflated their price, particularly in flow."
Movers in the London market include Rob Angel, a VP sales trader who has just joined Morgan Stanley after seven years at JPMorgan, where he most recently traded listed derivatives for hedge funds and clients in the Middle East. Angel did not respond to a request to comment for this article. Goldman Sachs recently hired Elena Su </news/elena-su>, an executive director (ED) in flow and exotic derivative sales from JPMorgan in Hong Kong.
Sources suggest that this year's market for equity derivatives hires is unusual to the extent that US banks are poaching from rival US houses, instead of pulling cheaper people from French banks. </news/french-equity-derivative-traders-are-more-popular-then-ever-not-just-with-banks>US bank employees tend to work with larger clients and can have a more immediate effect on revenues, but they cost more upfront.
One equity derivatives VP told us the packages on offer in the market are large and that people are being offered significant pay rises to move. "There is silly money around," he said. "Suddenly there's a lot of appetite to bid people up."
Morgan Stanley declined to comment for this article, but the bank is thought to have been among the more active recruiters among top US houses for equity derivatives this year. Following various buy-side departures </news/all-these-people-appear-to-be-escaping-morgan-stanley-s-emea-equity-derivatives-business> in EMEA after bonuses were paid, Morgan Stanley has not only added Angel from JPMorgan but Virgil Meyer </news/barclays-equity-derivatives-people-leaving>from Barclays in London and Henri Bussonnière, who was last seen at Nomura, in Hong Kong. Last year, JPMorgan's equities business outperformed </news/morgan-stanley-equities-traders> Morgan Stanley's in terms of revenue growth.
"Morgan Stanley are out there with all guns blazing," says one headhunter. "They're trying to backfill their vacancies with the best talent in the market." Next year they might be incentivised to pay existing VPs enough to stick around.

item.title: Jump Trading's ex-head of crypto trading in London joins forces with a young hedge fund manager
item.description:
After FTX </news/leopold-aschenbrenner-situational-awareness-sam-bankman-fried-ftx> crashed, major electronic trading firms recoiled from the crypto space but, in recent years, they've been dipping their toes back in. Jump Crypto </news/2023/10/jump-trading-crypto-kanav-kariya> is one such firm, and was reportedly expanding its US crypto trading operations last summer <https://www.coindesk.com/business/2025/03/05/trading-titan-jump-is-regrouping-its-u-s-crypto-efforts-insiders-say>. Its London trading head left around that time, and has since resurfaced at a crypto-native hedge fund.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Chris Drew has joined crypto hedge fund Fasanara Digital as its head of trading. He was previously head of London digital asset trading at Jump but left in 2025. Fasarana Digital is run by Nikita Fadeev, </news/nikita-fadeev> who founded the fund aged just 25 in 2021 </news/2022/06/crypto-hedge-fund-manager>. Drew is one of four hires that Fasanara has made in the past year.
Drew spent a total of 16 years at Jump Trading. He started out trading multi-asset strategies but began specializing in crypto in 2019, two years before the trading firm rebranded Jump Crypto as a different entity. The firm was accused of manipulating TerraUSD </news/terraform-labs-jane-street-bryce-pratt> in a lawsuit filed in 2023, but Drew, who was only appointed to a leadership role that year, did not face any allegations.
Before Jump, Drew was a quant trader at Sun Trading, an early player in the high-frequency trading </news/high-frequency-trading-hiring-and-pay>scene that was acquired by Hudson River Trading back in 2018. He was also a former spot FX trader at JPMorgan.
Nikita Fadeev told us that Drew's arrival is part of a broader push into "TradFi" markets as they "increasingly overlap" with crypto. He said that tokenized real world assets have more than doubled in market cap over the past year, particularly due to equities and commodities like metals and energy. Fasanara's not the only crypto firm making the leap; last week, Wintermute became eligible to become a market maker for securities exchanges like the New York Stock Exchange.

item.title: Morning Coffee: Ex-Goldman Sachs private equity associate embodies most desirable date. Fine times at the hedge fund that wants you in the office 5 days a week
item.description:
If you work in private equity </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-private-equity>, this could be your summer. By some quirk of fate, private equity guys (for they are mostly guys) have become the new more desirable boyfriends. So says the Wall Street Journal, <https://www.wsj.com/lifestyle/olivia-rodrigo-private-equity-boyfriend-fc331621?mod=e2tw> which notes that celebrities Reese Witherspoon, Nicole Kidman and Olivia Rodrigo have all achieved one.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
The men in question include Michael Reinstein, the founder of private equity firm Regent; Oliver Haarman, founder of London-based SearchLight Capital; and Julian Croonenberghs, a mere associate at HG in New York and former Goldman Sachs financial institutions group (FIG) analyst. Reinstein is dating Kidman. Haarman is dating Witherspoon. Rodrigo,a singer-songwriter and former child actress, is dating Croonenberghs.
Three celebrities don't make a trend but where some celebrities go, other mortals will follow. Kevin Cassidy, a 28-year-old former private-equity associate at New Mountain Capital disparaged the WSJ's suggestion that PE guys are the new hot dates, suggesting that he is not a beneficiary. But Johnny Hilbrant Partridge, who ruthlessly mocks private equity bros on Instagram, <https://www.instagram.com/johnnyhilbrant/?hl=en> said the industry has become synonymous with finance. On this basis, private equity professionals are just niche beneficiaries of the "man in finance" TikTok trend.
A well publicised study in the journal Evolution and Human Behavior <https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S109051381730315X> found that women are prepared to disregard male physical unattractiveness if men have higher pay. Private equity pay is falling by virtue of withered carried interest payments. </news/this-is-what-s-occurred-to-carried-interest-payments-at-blackstone-this-year>Fortunately, the PE professionals in question also appear to be tall, and so they will always have that in their favour.
Separately, we noted </news/bill-ackman>five months ago that Bill Ackman's Pershing Square seemed a nice place to work. Now Ackman has confirmed this.
Speaking to Fortune, <https://fortune.com/2026/08/05/pershing-square-ceo-bill-ackman-ai-investing-ipos-new-york-city-zohran-mamdani/>Ackman said he likes to have his 48 employees in the office "five days a week, ten months a year," but they are all very well rewarded. "We take care of our people, including their health—from how we filter the air, to the food in our cafe, to gym access and healthcare," he says. "Because of that, people don’t think about leaving. In the last decade, we haven’t had a single undesired departure from the firm, which is very unusual in this industry."
Ackman's employees, who are hired for their "highest character" are not paid on the basis of their P&L, but the P&L of the $35bn fund. If you occupy an investment role at Pershing Square, you will be expected to decamp to Bridgehampton on the east end of Long Island to work in the summer. Ackman has a large beachfront estate there, although it's not clear whether you will stay on his couch.
Meanwhile...
The new private equity investment trend is yacht marinas. CVC agreed to sell marina group D-Marin to French private equity firm InfraVia for around €1bn. They offer dependable cash flow and you can add perks like restaurants and lounges. (Financial Times) < https://www.ft.com/content/69c573e0-9c24-451d-bb13-ae7a7c3104c0?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Bank of America is spending $250m on drugs like Ozempic for its people. "We see a great impact on employees." (Business Insider) <https://www.businessinsider.com/bank-of-america-250-million-glp-1-ozempic-brian-moynihan-2026-8>
Chris Hohn </news/chris-hohn-hedge-fund> is a man unafraid to express his opinions. “Any idiot can see that the climate has changed and climate change is accelerating. Anybody who doesn’t look at the science is wilfully ignorant.” (The Times) <https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/article/chris-hohn-climate-change-net-zero-interview-rzwf3clj7>
Pay expenses at Goldman Sachs' London business were up 21% on the back of bigger bonus accruals in the first half of the year. (Financial News) <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/goldman-sachs-london-pay-costs-up-21-as-trading-revenue-jumps-0d226394>
This is what headhunters actually do. (ScienceDirect) <https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1162908826000472>
Should you wear shorts in the office? “Loins are only to be aired in gyms, pools, bathrooms, and bedrooms, unless the rest of the outfit is so chic that it elevates the loin rather than drawing attention to it. If you are not in the top 5 percent in terms of styling, then you probably can’t pull off different lengths on different occasions — you should stick to trousers.” (The Cut) <https://www.thecut.com/article/male-shorts-anxiety-summer.html?utm_source=twitter&utm_medium=s1&utm_campaign=nym>
In any normal year, financial services professionals leave Dubai in the summer. This year they left in March because of the war and are obliged to stay there in the summer to maintain residence visas, which are automatically cancelled after long periods outside the United Arab Emirates. (The Banker) <https://www.thebanker.com/content/48374c3f-252d-41a6-a066-2e7b9f5dcaf8>
Jane Street has got this competition to reverse engineer an ASIC (chip). (Jane Street) <https://blog.janestreet.com/can-you-reverse-engineer-an-asic/>

item.title: The Deutsche Bank MD who became a Reiki Master after a breakdown
item.description:
Paul Reeves is sitting at home in front of a camera. He is tanned and he is tattooed. Behind him is a statue of a Buddha. Ahead of him is his career as a master of the art of Reiki and dissipator of stress for people working in "high pressure industries." - People like Reeves himself until seven years ago.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Reeves spent 23 years working for Deutsche Bank from 1996 to 2019. He was a managing director (MD) during the formative and then difficult period for Deutsche's investment bank. At one point he was designated 'CF3 Chief Executive' with regulatory responsibility for Deutsche's UK operations. He was also chief operating officer and regional control officer Deutsche EMEA Bank's markets division.
It was a job that nearly broke him. Instead of having his career as a Reiki Master ahead of him, Reeves could have had nothing at all. "I went to work one day, refused to speak to anyone and locked myself in my office," he says. "They sent me home on the train and I tried to kill myself at Liverpool Street Station."
He survived. And now he wants to help other people in a situation like his own.
"I was under a lot of pressure both at work and in my home life," says Reeves. "At work, my career was split into two halves. In the first half, I was growing and developing new markets and businesses. In the second half I was making sure those businesses complied with regulations that were so complex it was difficult to make money. A lot of the systems had been created quickly and didn't hang together. You couldn't oversee what traders were doing and so I was implementing the controls structure that would create management reports."
It was a job that involved long hours and travel. Reeves says he found himself working 16-18 hour days as Deutsche's regulatory issues mounted. A senior colleague, William Broeksmit, Deutsche's former chief risk officer, took his own life in 2014. Reeves spent years concealing his troubles. He was medicated from 2009 to 2016 and constantly tried to underplay the issues with his mental health. "The attitude at the time was you get paid a lot of money. Don’t make a fuss. If you can’t handle it, resign," he says. "HR aren't there to help you, and I knew that as COO. They would just want to get someone like me out of the bank as quickly and cheaply as possible."
It didn't help that, throughout this period, Reeves' marriage was failing. He was the main breadwinner and he had high familial costs. His father died, and he says his now ex-wife wasn't sympathetic to his stress: "It's not easy when your partner just wants to know how you're going to pay the school fees."
Reeves ended up spending $750k in legal fees alone during his ensuing divorce. After hitting rock bottom at Deutsche Bank, he was diagnosed with bipolar disorder, and continued suffering in the years that followed. Until finally something changed.
"I went on holiday to the Maldives and I met a lady who was a guru working in the wellness area of the spa," says Reeves. "She was offering holistic treatment and she invited me to India for a retreat. It was something that found me, rather than something I was looking for. And it was incredibly comforting and awakening."
Reeves subsequently qualified as a Level 3 Reiki Master himself. Reiki is about working with the energy centres in the body, he says. Unlike massage, it involves working around 10cm away from the body's surface. Reeves says people can be sceptical, until they try it. "People say they feel much calmer after. Sometimes they see things. People tell me they have seen phoenixes and crows and all manner of different animals. Some feel they are levitating. Some say I am pressing down on them."
Looking back on his time at Deutsche Bank, he says he wishes he got out of the industry sooner. "In those first five years I couldn’t even bring myself to talk to anyone from the industry – it was almost like PTSD," he says.
Now Reeves wants to help people in the situation he was in. "It's not worth it. The money was great, but it's not worth the stress," he says.
If you or someone you know is struggling, support is available. In the UK, contact Samaritans free on 116 123. In the US, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline). In Singapore, contact SOS on 1-767 or text 9151 1767. In Hong Kong, contact The Samaritans on 2896 0000. Other countries can find a local helpline via findahelpline.com <https://findahelpline.com>.

item.title: The Coffee Run: How a 25-year-old who worked for Sam Bankman-Fried made and lost billions of dollars
item.description:
We've launched a new weekly video series <https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLqJc_c5JT66B3Cp_26xsN8Xsv2EtvtEQQ> to accompany Morning Coffee, in which we look at one story in more depth to give you the full picture.
Prior to founding Situtational Awareness, Leopold Aschenbrenner was most well-known for working at OpenAI, where he formed the thesis for his paper from which Situational Awareness got its name. You might not also know that he worked at FTX, the crypto firm of disgraced billionaire Sam Bankman-Fried.
Aschenbrenner and SBF are believers in the same ideology: effective altruism. Following revelations about how Situational Awareness made so much money, their situations have some slight similarities. Find out why on The Coffee Run.

item.title: Banks are wildly hiring investment bankers specialising in technology deals: "The landscape is huge"
item.description:
There was a time when if you were a technology investment banker </news/what-is-an-investment-bank>, you specialised in technology, broadly defined. That time has long passed. As technology has taken over everything, technology bankers have fragmented. They are now specialised in all manner of niches.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
As we reported yesterday </news/goldman-sachs-hired-a-barclays-financial-technology-banking-md-in-new-york>, Goldman Sachs just hired Barclays managing director (MD) Ben Froehlich as an MD for its 'financial technology' investment banking business. Also yesterday, Deutsche Bank hired Ed Liu </news/bank-of-america-m-a>, a 'software banker' at BofA as global head of TMT. Earlier in the week, Citi hired Rohan Sen from Bank of America for 'technology services' banking.
This is just a few days' hiring in the technology banking market. Search firm Sheffield Haworth says that in the US alone 62 managing directors (MDs) in software banking have changed jobs so far this year. They work across niches that include those above, plus categories like 'enterprise software', 'payments and digital assets,' 'supply chain technology,' 'internet,' 'digital media,' 'semi-conductors,' and 'AI.'
Speaking off the record, one senior technology banker said this year's explosion of technology banking recruitment reflects the sheer size of the market for technology deals. "The landscape is huge and has fragmented," he says. "A number of smaller boutiques have also begun to compete more meaningfully on the bigger deals where the bulge brackets care, so the big banks are adding coverage."
Dealogic says technology was the biggest sector for global M&A in the first half of 2025, and that it remained the biggest sector for global M&A in the first half of 2026, generating around $4.5bn in revenues for banks. The second largest sector, healthcare, generated just under $4bn. The third largest, financial institutions, generated just over $2bn. Technology is huge.
This might be why M&A recruitment firm Prospect Rock Partners suggested in March <https://prospectrockpartners.com/prospect-rock-partners-2025-ib-compensation-report/> that pay for technology and TMT bankers is often more generous than in other groups, particularly in the junior and mid-vice president (VP) levels, where it can be up to 10% higher.
In the US, Sheffield Haworth says this year's biggest hirers of technology bankers have been Citi, which has recruited eight other bankers in addition to Sen (Alex Berkett, Gaddy Cohen, Anand Govind, Chris Grosse, Anand Agarwal, Dhruv Fotadar, Florian M Plath, and Josh Sheets) and Wells Fargo, which has recruited six (Badhri Varanasi, Matthew Lacy, Jesse Chasse, Derrick Chao, Jusung Juice Kwok, and Mark Gracia). BofA also recruited four bankers, including Gary Kirkham from Centerview and Richard Hardegree from UBS.
Many of this year's senior US technology banker hires haven't been in their new seats long. Sheffield Haworth says nearly 30% of them only arrived in their jobs from July onwards. Some, like Jason Rowe, whom bank of America hired from Goldman Sachs as global co-head of technology banking (possibly prompting Liu's departure for a similar role at Deutsche Bank) in March, are only due to arrive in September 2026 after a pleasant summer off.
Hiring a lot of senior bankers is often followed by hiring a lot of junior and mid-ranking bankers. One MD in the technology space says he's been receiving two to three headhunter calls a week. This may soon apply to everyone in the market.

item.title: AI is changing private equity jobs. This is how
item.description:
Private equity </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-private-equity> firms are infused with artificial intelligence. They are using it to supercharge the work of private equity professionals. They are also investing heavily in the AI industry.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Private capital firms are pouring money into the broad AI universe. In mid-2026, Blackstone alone <https://www.blackstone.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/blackstone-secure/Office-of-the-CIO-2026-Mid-Year-Investment-Perspectives.pdf?v=1783606609> said it would invest $100bn in its data centre portfolio by the end of 2026, and around $300bn in AI chip production over the same period.
AI is also transforming the way that jobs in private equity are done. Even in mid-2024, AI was already being used to help private equity firms source companies to invest in, to screen whether the potential investments were any good and to do due diligence by investigating the claims companies made about their performance.
Speaking in May 2026, John Stecher, Blackstone's CTO, said <https://www.blackstone.com/insights/article/ai-at-scale-a-conversation-with-blackstones-cto-and-global-head-of-the-operating-team/> AI is allowing the firm to sift through and initially evaluate potential investments incredibly quickly. "What used to be a weekend-long activity can now be carried out in minutes," said Stecher. "We’re also using AI at the very top of the funnel... AI allows us to evaluate opportunities faster, say no faster, and spend more time on what we believe are the highest-quality investments."
KPMG also noted <https://kpmg.com/de/en/media/press-releases/2026/03/m-a-market-2026-private-equity-drives-the-upturn-carve-outs-in-focus-ai-transforms-deals.html> in May that when AI is used for tasks like competitor analysis and internal financials analysis, the time taken can go from weeks to just a few days.
Because PE firms can use AI to screen huge numbers of potential firms at the top of the funnel, human judgement is needed further down the investment process. Just because an AI says something is a good investment, this doesn't mean the investment will happen. Humans have the ultimate sign-off.
PE firms also use AI to improve the companies they're investing in. In May 2026, Bain Capital struck an agreement with Open AI to integrate AI across its portfolio companies. Bain said <https://www.bain.com/about/media-center/press-releases/2026/bain-company-openai-a-new-venture-to-deploy-ai-at-enterprise-scale/> that portfolio companies will focus on top-line growth, through "faster product development and improved customer experience".
AI can make a big difference. A report from consulting firm BCG <https://www.bcg.com/assets/2025/executive-perspectives-ai-first-companies-private-equity.pdf> published in January 2026 gave examples of how AI improved operations at portfolio companies. An asset manager improved its customer service; a beauty company “redefined” its supply chain. The former reduced expenses by 30%, and the latter reduced logistics costs by 3%.
“AI is rapidly becoming one of the most important value-creation opportunities across the portfolio,” said Bain’s midyear 2026 private equity report <https://www.bain.com/insights/private-equity-midyear-report-2026/>. “Cost reduction efforts are often an early focus, but AI is also accelerating product development, improving sales and customer acquisition, enhancing pricing sophistication,” among others.
It's not all positive, though. As we noted last year </news/artificial-intelligence-use-banking> AI may reduce the need for private equity juniors to screen deals, and it can kill potential investments. - Not directly by screening them out, but because generative is changing the operating environment and means some companies are no longer viable.
After Claude Cowork was introduced in February 2026, software stocks plummeted around 25% on their highs of the previous 12 months amidst fears that AI itself would replace software. Private credit funds like Blue Owl and Apollo </news/ares-blue-owl-carlyle-results> had invested in firms such as Amazon aggregator Perch </news/jpmorgan-bankers-pressure-2026>, which caused investors to attempt to redeem their money, and in turn led to a pause on redemptions.
As AI eats everything, private equity firms are increasingly hiring experts in the technology. Apollo, for example, has an active job posting <https://www.dice.com/job-detail/a1f51e9b-2aa9-42a8-be5a-dfc4f2bcd744> on its website for an "AI Solutions & Quantitative Strategist" associate, which expects applicants to "serve as a bridge" between the firm's quants and hybrid investing team, "ensuring that AI initiatives are practical, high-impact and embedded into day-to-day workflows."

item.title: There are three investment banks, and there is everyone else
item.description:
If you want to work in investment banking </news/the-investment-banking-recruitment-process>, you have your choice of firms. Big banks, little banks </news/boutique-investment-banks>, medium sized banks. In reality, however, there may only be three banks that matter.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Market intelligence provider Tricumen analysed the operating revenue per front-office </news/front-office-middle-office-back-office-banking> full-time employee big investment banks in H1 of 2026. As the spider chart below shows, the employees of just three banks could be considered "above average" in performance for "capital markets activities." Those three banks were JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, and Morgan Stanley.
The charts below indicated the average performance per individuals within a banking group. The dotted, circular line on each chart below indicates the average performance across the peer group average. Anything inside the dotted line is worse than average; anything outside is better. “Capital markets </news/capital-markets-jobs-ecm-and-dcm>” is defined as all investment banking activity. That includes the “banking” category (which includes both M&A </news/get-a-job-in-ma> and debt/equity capital markets </news/capital-markets-jobs-ecm-and-dcm>), as well as fixed income, currencies, and commodities (FICC) and equities trading </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank>.
Operating Revenue per front-office full-time employee, H1 2026
Goldman Sachs was the best bank for "banking" specifically. It benefited from an exceptionally strong investment banking </news/the-investment-banking-recruitment-process> performance in H1 of 2026, with revenue growing by 52% compared to the same period last year. At the same time, its headcount declined from 47,000 to 46,200 in the same period - Goldman had leaner teams that performed better.
Within sales & trading </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank>, performance was more mixed, with Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan’s fixed income, currencies, and commodities traders performing well. Within equities, both JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley’s equities traders were well above average.
JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, and Morgan Stanley of course have another important distinction: they’re the biggest investment banks in the world, by quite some margin. According to market intelligence provider Dealogic, which aggregated year-to-date investment banking revenue, these three combined captured around a quarter of global wallet share in the industry.

item.title: Morning Coffee: Bank of America hired all kinds of new M&A MDs, but some special old ones are leaving. Millennium loves Anthropic
item.description:
Bank of America's investment bank has transformed itself into a hiring magnet. But while it attracts tens of new managing directors (MDs) in M&A, some of its most prized existing bankers are slipping out the door.
Speaking yesterday, Matthew Koder, the now-longstanding head of Bank of America's global corporate and investment bank, said <https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/bank-americas-co-head-investment-banking-mike-joo-leave-firm-memo-says-2026-08-06/> the bank has added "more than 40 new managing directors" this year. Those figures are presumably global, but in July alone BofA made nine "senior hires" for its 200 person US middle market <https://newsroom.bankofamerica.com/content/newsroom/press-releases/2026/07/bank-of-america-expands-regional-investment-banking-coverage--ad.html> banking team and proclaimed that it discerned a "significant opportunity" in that area.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
It seems unfortunate, then, that the person who made that proclamation is now leaving. Reuters <https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/bank-americas-co-head-investment-banking-mike-joo-leave-firm-memo-says-2026-08-06/>reported yesterday that Mike Joo, BofA's co-head of investment banking, is leaving for an unspecified external opportunity.
Joo had spent 20 years at BofA and was named co-head of M&A <https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/bofa-names-faiz-ahmad-mike-joo-co-heads-investment-banking-memo-says-2025-08-20/> with Faiz Ahmad only last August. The BofA memo announcing Joo's appointment in August 2025 said he would continue to prioritize BofA's middle market clients. Ahmad seemed more oriented internationally.
Joo isn't the only slippage. Also this week, BofA lost Amy Lissauer, its prized activist defence banker, who will soon <https://www.ft.com/content/62b70b3a-88c9-4d6c-bc0c-b840586af91a?syn-25a6b1a6=1> be joining JPMorgan. Lissauer, who joined BofA from Evercore in 2019, had built its activist defence business into one of the best.
BofA has also lost an array of other less meaty senior bankers, including Ed Liu, who is joining Deutsche as head of TMT banking (and who also resigned this week), and Rohan Sen, who's going to Citi.
What is occurring? Maybe nothing at all. It's a busy year for M&A and it's not unusual for M&A bankers to be wooed by rival banks. It's also worth noting, though, that there were years recently when Bank of America didn't seem to hire many new managing directors (MDs) for its US investment bank. In 2024, for example, it seemed to lose </news/bank-of-america-barclays-and-goldman-sachs-need-new-us-bankers-this-year>a lot of banking MDs in America without hiring many replacements. In 2025, it made a few more hires </news/md-hiring-investment-banks>, but not loads. This year's 40 new hires seem a lot in comparison. They include the likes of Jason Rowe, from Goldman Sachs who is BofA's new head of technology banking, and Gary Kirkham, who left to become a partner at Centerview in 2021, but is now back in the fold.
With Joo gone, BofA's M&A business is now run by Ahmad, who has an eclectic past <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/newsletters/2022-12-02/bank-of-america-s-faiz-ahmad-looks-for-a-different-kind-of-deal-to-support-the-bank> in transaction services, high yield, structured finance and commodities trading. Ahmad will be assisted by Karim Assef, a BofA veteran of 30 years who has not left and is the chair of global investment banking.
Separately, if you really love Anthropic, you might get privileged access to frontier models and that would be a fine thing.
Millennium </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-hedge-fund-millennium> really loves Anthropic. Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-06/millennium-partners-with-anthropic-to-develop-ai-risk-analyst?utm_source=website&utm_medium=share&utm_campaign=twitter> reports that the hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job>is collaborating with Anthropic as part of its AI lab and that the two are working together to build a "digital risk analyst." This analyst, which is described as a "tool" rather than as a colleague, will reportedly assist Millennium's humans to make decisions and extract risk insights across asset classes.
Millennium's enthusiasm for Anthropic is not restricted to risk. It's reportedly also using Anthropic's products to write software, build products and improve workflows.
Given that Millennium is increasingly ingesting other hedge funds <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-04-27/jain-global-to-return-cash-exclusively-manage-millennium-money>by virtue of its large pool of capital and advanced back office </news/front-office-middle-office-back-office-banking>and trading systems, integrating Anthropic's solutions might help it cut costs. As we noted yesterday, Jain Global's operations staff have reportedly </news/hedge-fund-jain-global-hired-morgan-stanley-s-head-of-high-yield-trading-in-london> been guaranteed compensation until the end of 2026. Maybe Anthropic will replace them after that?
Meanwhile...
Javier Velazquez left Millennium in London to found hedge fund Albar in 2018. Millennium gave him initial capital. Now he's returning external clients' cash and managing money entirely for Millennium after generating returns of only 1.1% so far this year. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-06/hedge-fund-albar-is-returning-cash-to-run-only-millennium-money?utm_source=website&utm_medium=share&utm_campaign=twitter>
Jane Street is shifting its $11bn in debt to investors including Pimco Private in a credit deal that will allow it to make further investments in AI while also reducing its need to keep disclosing financials to its debt holders. Borrowing privately usually costs at least 0.25 percentage points more. (Financial Times) <https://www.ft.com/content/80f5fede-a34a-4069-a751-f9523e3c6e00?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Hackers devised websites aimed at stealing passwords from employees of private equity firms and companies including Blackstone, Bridgewater Associates, Apollo Global Management, Bain Capital, KKR, TPG, CME Group and Moody's. (Reuters) <https://www.reuters.com/world/hackers-targeted-us-private-equity-other-firms-including-blackstone-cme-data-2026-08-06/>
The new hacking nightmare for financial services firms. “Before they could attack 50 entities in a targeted attack, now they can do 1,00. Hackers can also listen into a phone call and mimic the voice, tone and phrasings of the speakers to create fake calls.” (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-05/major-hedge-funds-targeted-in-wave-of-attempted-cyberattacks>
America is offering to print dollars to buy yen. It’s not quite quantitative easing. The Federal Reserve lends Japan money in return for temporary ownership of Treasurys in repurchase agreements, rather than outright buying the Treasurys. But like QE it expands the Fed balance sheet and pumps billions of dollars into the economy. (WSJ) <https://www.wsj.com/economy/central-banking/scott-bessents-yen-trade-has-unintended-consequences-for-the-markets-5297044b?mod=panda_wsj_author_alert>
Hedge funds in Florida keep hiring PhDs. (Kronor Group) <https://kronorgroup.com/florida-hedge-funds-keep-reeling-in-newly-minted-phds/>
First you take Ozempic, then you get "Ozempic face", then you have to inject fat to look normal again. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-05/can-k-beauty-fix-ozempic-face-one-firm-plans-skin-booster-made-with-human-fat?taid=6a73e146fbc22200014f425e&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
Established” LinkedIn users (100+ connections) who made retroactive edits to the description of jobs they’d already left between 2020 and 2026 tended to play up how much they used artificial intelligence tools in previous roles, while de-emphasising DEI. (Financial Times) <https://www.ft.com/content/4a4b442c-7ae4-4553-bcab-d744d8d46c79>
Leopold Aschenbrenner's new $400m investment is in an unnamed company backed by Sequoia Capital. Alfred Lin, a partner at Sequoia, likes Leopold. He says: “He’s really good. He’s going to be around.” (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-06/aschenbrenner-s-400-million-bet-went-to-sequoia-backed-company?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=260806&utm_campaign=author_17940573>

item.title: Quant hedge fund Two Sigma raised average pay to £500k in one of its London entities
item.description:
Two Sigma has had an unusual few years. It was once regarded as the chillest hedge fund </news/2023/02/two-sigma-jobs-culture>to work for but, after some job cuts in 2024 </news/two-sigma-job-cuts> and a very public squabble </news/two-sigma-is-still-the-fun-hedge-fund-despite-its-founders-squabbles> between its co-founders, it has slightly lost its sheen. Despite this, accounts for one of its London entities </news/best-paying-hedge-funds> suggests that the hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> is paying more than ever.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
'Two Sigma International' released accounts for 2025 via Companies House this week. Average 'salaries and wages' at the entity were £503k ($676k), up 34% from 2024, in which it paid £377k. Its principal activity is to "provide investment management and administration services for certain hedge funds and other affiliated investment companies."
The entity reported a slight decline in headcount from 93 to 85. Those employees may not have left and instead been moved to the fund's other entity, Two Sigma Securities UK, which has yet to declare accounts. However that entity declares its principal activity as proprietary trading, and appears to be associated with Two Sigma's separate market making </news/high-frequency-trading-hiring-and-pay#:~:text=Electronic%20Market%20Making,hedge%20their%20risk.>arm. In 2024, it had 14 employees and paid them an average of £608k.
Two Sigma is hiring in London in 2026. In March, </news/two-sigma-new-office-london>the fund moved into a new office near Liverpool Street, occupying one floor while renovating another to make room for more. It currently has eight vacancies; this includes openings for Two Sigma Securities which is "entering an exciting growth phase."

item.title: "I work in TMT investment banking for a European bank. It is a nightmare. No one seems to care"
item.description:
I am a junior investment banker working in the technology, media and telecoms team of a European bank in London. Life in this team is a nightmare and many of my colleagues have left.
The bank doesn't seem to care. Over the past year we've lost around ten analysts from the broader team and this just seems to be considered the norm. No one in a management position seems to be asking why.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
People have left for private equity </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-private-equity>, for sovereign wealth funds and for rival banks. Maybe this is just what happens, but I know that some people have also had medical issues because of the amount we are expected to work.
The problem here begins and ends with a few managing directors (MDs). There is no electronic system for monitoring working hours here and some of the MDs seem to think it's fine to make their juniors work crazy hours. There have been complaints and reg flags have been raised but nothing ever gets done about it.
People are therefore leaving with their feet, or risking their physical and mental health. I thought it wasn't like this in 2026. It's ruining young people's careers from the start.

item.title: Hedge fund Jain Global hired Morgan Stanley's head of high yield trading in London
item.description:
When we revealed this week that Jon Stead, </news/jon-stead-morgan-stanley> the head of high yield trading at Morgan Stanley, had resigned from the bank, we suggested that he might be joining hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> Point72.
We were wrong. Stead will instead be joining hedge fund Jain Global. </news/hedge-funds-are-becoming-colder-darker-less-forgiving>
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Jain Global declined to comment and Stead did not respond to our requests for comment. However, multiple sources confirmed that his destination will be Jain.
We understand that Stead might help Jain set up a new European high yield trading business. Maybe he will hire some more people? Maybe they will also come from Morgan Stanley, where the credit team has been leaking talent </news/morgan-stanley-credit-traders-leaving> for a while? Jain Global has a history of hiring credit traders from Morgan Stanley: the bank's former head of European credit trading Herbert Filho </news/morgan-stanley-s-european-head-of-credit-trading-left-jain-global> arrived on June 3rd 2025 and left again in early February, possibly for personal reasons.
Jain Global was founded by Bobby Jain </news/as-jain-global-p-ms-take-headhunter-calls-bobby-jain-explains-why-they-need-patience>, a former co-chief investment officer at Millennium. It launched in July 2024 with $5.3bn and delivered returns of only 0.5% in the half year of 2024 and only 3.7% in 2025 as it began deploying capital. So far this year, it has generated returns of 3.9% according to Bloomberg. <https://x.com/nishantkumar07/status/2085020521800864130?s=20>Citadel CEO Ken Griffin suggested last month </news/ken-griffin-hedge-fund>that hedge funds currently need to generate returns in excess of 8.55% to keep investors happy. Fortunately Jain Global will now be managing money exclusively for Millennium <https://www.blackstone.com/insights/article/ai-at-scale-a-conversation-with-blackstones-cto-and-glo…>, which is familiar with Bobby Jain's talents.
Unusually, Jain Global launched with seven different strategies. These included: fundamental, quantitative and arbitrage in the equities business; rates, macro and credit in fixed income; plus Asia. Speaking earlier this year, Bobby Jain referred to the approach as a "seven-legged-stool."
Jain Global has also invested heavily in infrastructure. Business Insider <https://www.businessinsider.com/jain-global-millennium-deal-details-equity-unit-exits-2026-5> reported in May that Jain's back office staff have been guaranteed compensation until the end of 2026.

item.title: A high-frequency trading firm just hired Bjarne Stroustrup, creator of C++
item.description:
Electronic trading firms </news/high-frequency-trading-hiring-and-pay> work on low latency trading systems which, nine times out of ten, are written in C++. </news/finance/c-coding-language-problems> Trading firms can pay over $500k </news/low-latency-c> for elite engineers who can get the most out of the language; at Susquehanna, those engineers will now be working with the man who invented C++.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Bjarne Stroustrup </news/c-java-bjarne-stroustrup> announced via LinkedIn that he has joined Susquehanna as a technical fellow on a part time basis. A press release seen by eFinancialCareers states that Stroustrup will be "helping shape the optimization and evolution of the firm’s codebase."
It's not his first role in finance; Stroustrup spent eight years in banking with Morgan Stanley </news/2020/12/bjarne-stroustrup-morgan-stanley> where he was an MD and tech fellow working on "foundational software." He left in 2022, and has since been a full-time professor at Columbia University.
Stroustrup said in the release that "financial software places extraordinary demands on performance, reliability, and maintainability, making it one of the most interesting applications of modern software engineering." He said that he will "explore new ways to apply modern C++ to increasingly complex systems" through his work at Susquehanna.
It seems likely that his role will be similar to that of Herb Sutter at Citadel Securities; </news/citadel-securities-c-plus-plus-job-skills> Sutter became the market maker's first tech fellow in 2024, </news/herb-sutter-citadel-securities>joining from Microsoft to lead training initiatives and increase broader engagement with C++ within the firm. Sutter also still works closely with the C++ standards committee and it seems Stroustrup will do the same; Soma Bockelman, Susquehanna's global head of technology, said that the firm is "excited to contribute to the continued advancement of the C++ community while further strengthening the engineering capabilities that power our business."
Roughly half of Susquehanna's 244 open job listings mention C++. Some of the highest paying roles are for engineers working on low latency architecture. Stroustrup said on a podcast earlier this year </news/using-english-as-a-coding-language-won-t-get-you-a-600k-programming-job> that these roles are unlikely to be replaced by AI </news/how-ai-is-affecting-careers-in-electronic-trading-and-hft>; he said AI generated C++ code in a low-latency context can be "bloated" and is less secure than human-written code.

item.title: How much do electronic trading jobs really pay?
item.description:
Electronic trading firms, HFTs and market makers </news/high-frequency-trading-hiring-and-pay>are some of the most lucrative places to work in finance today. The top firms are paying more than $2m per head </news/jane-street-employees> for talented employees to power their high-tech trading </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank> systems. But where (and in what roles) can you earn the most?
What are salaries like in electronic trading?
Salaries in the space are impressive but not ridiculous. We broke down average pay for research </news/what-is-a-quant-researcher-hedge-fund>, engineering </news/how-to-get-a-technology-job-bank> and trading staff at various top firms using salaries filed on the H1B visa </news/h1b-visa-changes-goldman-sachs> salary database since the start of 2024; the data showed that even the most elite firms didn't pay above $300k on average.
Jane Street and Citadel Securities </news/citadel-securities-vs-jane-street> paid average salaries of $266k and $244k respectively. In both firms, roles for research and trading staff were higher than those working in engineering.
What are bonuses like in electronic trading?
When bonuses are added, total pay is much greater. Average total compensation globally for Jane Street's ~3500 employees was $2.7m <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-05-01/jane-street-pay-pool-hits-9-4-billion-more-than-doubles-in-2025> in 2025. Jane Street has a sizeable support team working in areas like graduate recruitment </news/jane-street-target-universities> and accounting; those employees likely earn far less than that figure, which would suggest that front office traders are earning even more. Citadel Securities, meanwhile, paid ~$2.1m </news/citadel-securities-pay-2m> to its employees that year.
Other firms have generally been able to keep their pay under wraps but, through the UK's Companies House, we can see how much firms spend on pay in London and how many people they employ (giving us average pay per head). Our full breakdown is visible here; </news/hft-pay-london>most firms have not reported their compensation for last year, but in 2024 most of the top firms paid between £450k and £850k. Quadrature, </news/high-paying-quant-development-jobs-quadrature> a London-based trading firm, paid a massive £2.8m ($3.8m). Jane Street paid £808k ($1.1m) on average in 2024; global average pay that year was $1.4m.
The way bonuses are paid at these firms varies in both their allocation and distribution. Jane Street is thought to pay bonuses based on the performance of the firm </news/jane-street-is-a-bit-communist-in-the-way-it-pays-traders> rather than of individuals, and gives staff limited visibility of their individual PnL. Citadel Securities is thought to pay more in line with individual performance. Optiver offers a profit share tied to individual performance, in which staff earn 'marbles' </news/hft-optiver-uk-pay#:~:text=A%20key%20selling,its%20UK%20entity.> that correlate to a small percentage of Optiver's total profits that year.
Jane Street pays bonuses annually, but some firms pay them at multiple points across the year. IMC Trading says it pays bonuses semi-annually, whereas firms like Hudson River Trading and Radix Trading are known to pay bonuses quarterly.
The nature of these bonuses may be changing. These firms are usually 'prop trading firms' meaning that they trade using their own money and have historically been able to pay bonuses in all cash. At Jane Street, however, there are signs that the firm might be shifting to "long term incentive structures," </news/jane-street-pay-2026> where pay could be calculated using unspecified "complex formulas."
How much do interns earn in electronic trading?
Read more: 2027 summer intern pay at electronic trading firms: Where you can earn $10,000 per week </news/electronic-trading-summer-internship-pay>
Electronic trading firms and market makers are almost unequivocally the highest paying companies for interns. </news/highest-paying-internships-finance>Only some of the biggest hedge funds can compete. At the top end, it's common for quant interns and AI researchers </news/ai-researcher-pay-culture> to earn $5.8k per week, the equivalent of a $300k salary, without including sign-on bonuses.
Those sign-ons can also be massive. Hudson River Trading, which accepts 0.1% of applicants </news/hudson-river-trading-intern-pay>, pays Python engineering interns in New York a $25k signing bonus on top of a salary worth $5.8k per week. Optiver disclosed a total compensation of up to $100k for PhD </news/do-you-need-a-phd-for-a-quant-job-in-finance> quant interns. Not bad for a few months work.

item.title: Goldman Sachs hired a Barclays financial technology banking MD in Chicago
item.description:
Goldman Sachs has historically liked to grow its managing directors in-house. But where homegrown talent is not available, it will hire externally. It has just hired Ben Froehlich, a Barclays lifer.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Froehlich just joined Goldman in Chicago as a managing director in the specific niche of financial technology investment banking. He didn't respond to a request to comment for this article; nor did Goldman. FINRA says he's still technically at Barclays.
Froehlich joined Barclays as a summer intern in 2011 and made MD at the bank in 2022. He was initially in leveraged finance but moved into financial technology in 2021.
Financial technology bankers </news/2021/11/how-to-become-a-fintech-banker>are like a combination of financial institutions group (FIG) bankers and tech bankers. At Barclays, Joel Fleck, the co-head of FIG banking also has responsibility for financial technology. At Goldman Sachs, Marine Epailly, an MD of financial technology in London (also hired from Barclays eight years ago) has a background in TMT banking at Rothschild.
Jeff Gido, a veteran fintech banker, runs Goldman Sachs' financial technology group globally. In April, Gido was also appointed co-chair of Goldman's FIG group. Kelly Galanis, a Goldman Sachs lifer and partner, runs the fintech group for the firm in the US.

item.title: When a hedge fund boss calls to offer you a job, it may not be them
item.description:
If Ken Griffin </news/ken-griffin-citadel-culture>really likes you and really wants to hire you for Citadel, his hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job>, he might interview you personally. He might journey to see you. Maybe he will even call you and offer you the job. Griffin is famously <https://colossus.com/episode/384-ken-griffin-founder-of-citadel-and-citadel-securities/>said to have called Jon Arnold, the former head of Enron's gas trading team in 2002, in an attempt to hire him for the fund. Former Citadel CTO Umesh Subramanian </news/umesh-subramanian>also declared a partiality for calling "in-demand" candidates he wanted to hire.
But the call may not be from Ken, or from anyone else at Citadel. Similarly, if you receive a call from the likes of Jamie Dimon at JPMorgan, Steve Cohen at Point72 or Jonathan Gray at Blackstone, begging you to join, you should be circumspect. Events of yesterday suggest that telephone calls are not always what they seem.
Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-05/major-hedge-funds-targeted-in-wave-of-attempted-cyberattacks>reported yesterday that Two Sigma, Citadel, Millennium and several private equity firms were attacked by hackers using voice phishing. The Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/1fcca000-d9ac-4b3b-9d31-2fef0d1f55f3?syn-25a6b1a6=1>said the attacks involved impersonations of 'a trusted person or colleague through phone calls.' The firms involved did not appear to have been breached and have not commented for this article.
The audio phishing attack was unrelated to recruitment, but given the explosion of recruitment scams in the financial services sector, it's not inconceivable that the next level will involve Griffin calling with a job if you first wire him $1k. JPMorgan's chief AI recruiter <https://uk.trustpilot.com/review/efinancialcareers.com> in London already claimed someone was impersonating him (by email) a few weeks ago. Point72 has been targeted by recruitment scammers for nearly a decade. </news/2017/02/point72-asset-management-warns-applicants-on-new-recruitment-scam>
Google <https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/ai-vulnerability-exploitation-initial-access> noted earlier this year that scammers had begun appropriating "high-fidelity audio artifacts to impersonate authoritative figures." Senior financial services figures like Griffin, Dimon and Gray feature frequently in podcasts and on YouTube, making cloning their voices easy.
The era of the executive podcast may therefore be coming to an end. Either that, or there will soon be thousands of them, each generated by an AI explaining how to get a job at Citadel or JPMorgan in the voices of senior leaders.
